Mr. HUGUES LAPOINTE (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence) moved the second reading of Bill No. 394, to amend the Department of National Defence Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1-Moneys to cease to belong to Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO RELEASE FUNDS CONTRIBUTED AT EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
I understand that the purpose of this bill is to enable certain moneys, which were made available by the members of the various officers training corps throughout the country to promote the efficiency of their corps, to be released from the consolidated revenue fund and to be placed in the hands of trustees so that they may be used for their original purposes.
Before and during the war it had been the custom for officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the officers training corps to assign pay received from the Department of National Defence for various purposes, such as the building of drill halls and armouries, and so forth. That practice was wholly commendable, and the moneys had been set aside for that specific purpose. Apparently these moneys have recently been placed in the consolidated revenue fund, and the intention of this amendment is to provide that they shall be made available for the original purpose. With that
I heartily agree. But yesterday I asked the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence whether moneys derived from canteen sources were placed in these funds which it is -now proposed to release from the consolidated revenue fund. The parliamentary assistant informed me then that there were no such moneys derived from canteens, but he advised me during the day that this statement was not correct; that a small percentage, some three per cent, of the total moneys was derived from canteens which were run by these officers training corps.
I am' afraid that presents this bill in rather a different light. The committee will no doubt recall that only last year we had a committee on army canteen funds. Those funds were placed1 in an army benevolent fund which was to be administered under the chairmanship of the late Major-General Browne for the benefit of the men of the army who returned from the war and who were eligible to receive portions of this fund for the purpose for which it was created. I wonder whether the portion of these moneys which was derived from the canteen funds should not be placed in the army benevolent fund as were the funds which were derived from other canteens of units of the non-permanent militia, as they were called in the pre-war days.
There was a great deal of feeling at one time that the non-permanent units would like to administer and use for the benefit of the men who passed through them, or for promotion of the efficiency of their particular units, the funds accumulated in the canteens which they had operated. For instance, the highland1 units were anxious to obtain kilts; other units perhaps thought it would be a good thing to obtain instruments for regimental bands, or to promote the efficiency of their reserve army unit at the conclusion of the war. I am not sure that we are right in assigning to these purposes the money which came from canteens w'hen we have denied to the units of the nonpermanent militia or reserve army the right to utilize their canteen funds for their own particular purposes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO RELEASE FUNDS CONTRIBUTED AT EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Nanaimo pointed out, yesterday in the course of the explanation I gave at the resolution stage I answered a question of the hon. gentleman as to whether any of the funds affected by this legislation were canteen funds. My reply was in the negative. Later I was informed that a small percentage was canteen funds. However, I wish to point out that the benevolent fund to which my hon. friend has just referred, which was created last year by an act of this parliament, affected only canteen funds of the active force, and that no canteen funds
5698	COMMONS
Department of National Defence Act
of reserve force units were placed in the benevolent fund. The canteen funds of the C.O.T.C. were those of a strictly reserve unit which, under the act creating the benevolent fund, would not be included.
I might add that the action now being taken by the department is the expressed wish of all the C.O.T.C. units which existed during the war, numbering some twenty-eight. Since the end of the war they have repeatedly pressed the department for the release of these funds from the consolidated revenue fund, to be used for their original purposes. In some instances the amounts are considerable. In some cases the entire amount was collected through voluntary assigned pay on the part of the members of the corps, and substantial subscriptions by private individuals and bodies for memorial purposes, or for building accommodation strictly for the use of that particular contingent. The department has taken the view that considering the circumstances which existed in connection with a C.O.T.C. unit, which are quite different from those of the ordinary reserve units, the funds should be remitted in trust to the units concerned, to be used for the purposes for which they were originally collected. For instance, in one particular case all the members going through the particular C.O.T.C. unit-and I understand some 8.000 went through during the war-assigned their pay, both headquarters and camp pay, for the purpose of building a memorial to the C.O.T.C. of the particular university. I believe the wish of those men, who could have drawn their pay and then subscribed it to a particular fund with the same result, should now be acceded to.

Nothing was done in connection with the reserve army to recover any money unexpended at the end of the war, and I believe the C.O.T.C. units need encouragement and money. If through economy and good management they were able to save some money, I see no reason why it should be paid back to the government. They should be allowed to retain all the money for the benefit of the unit.

The difference is that the sums we are now trying to release consist in large part of pay and allowances and subscriptions by individuals, not by the government. Just what is the method of accounting with respect to the unexpended portion of governmental grants is something I could not say. I dare say that if they are

speechtext:
Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider Bill No. 338, respecting income taxes.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
Sections 1 to 5 inclusive agreed to.
On section 6-Dividends, annuities, etc.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer to paragraph (j), about which I believe the minister has received representations. It reads:
Amounts received by the taxpayer in the year that were dependent upon use of or production from property whether or not they were instalments of the sale price of the property, but instalments of the sale price of agricultural land shall not be included by virtue of this paragraph.
Income Tax Act

I know the hon. member for Calgary West wishes to speak to this paragraph. It has been brought to my attention that under this paragraph royalties on oil wells are being taxed not as capital but as income. Let me point out that the so-called royalties are in effect the capital of the person receiving them. Why is this form of capital singled out for the treatment indicated in the paragraph? It seems to me that the taxing authorities have a feeling that this is a sort of bonanza or windfall which may come to a person concerned, and therefore in a rough fashion this is a process of taking a slice of the receipts. I suggest that that is an inadequate reason for departing from ordinary taxation procedure. It may be in the minds of the government that people are getting huge windfalls and that therefore they should not be greatly concerned about the tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not quite clear as to the facts the hon. member may have in mind, but I am informed that there is no change in the law respecting the taxation of royalties. Oil royalties as such are and always have been subject to tax, with the appropriate deductions for depletion.
This section is not designed to tax oil royalties as such. It is really intended to effect a transaction which is an exchange of rights for royalties which are income. I am told there is no change in the substantive law. The pertinent section in the law, as my hon. friend probably knows, is section 3 (1) (f), which defines, as being included in income-
Rents, royalties, annuities or other like periodical receipts which depend upon production or use of any real or persona] property notwithstanding that the same are payable on account of the use or sale of any such property.
I have been assured by the law officers of the Department of Justice that there is no change in the substantive law.

I did not intend to suggest there was a change contemplated at the present time. My understanding is that the change was made earlier. Originally an attempt was made to tax oil as revenue, and this was ruled out. There was a case which tested that procedure, with which the minister is no doubt familiar. In that case the privy council held that the sale of oil was the realization of a capital asset and therefore was not subject to taxation. I understand that thereafter the legislation was altered. I presume the wording is the same as that which we have now.
The point I raise now is the principle involved. Surely the minister will agree that in substance this is a taxation of capital. This oil which comes out of the ground is a wasting

asset. Why should we tax this capital any more than any other kind? How can it be suggested that this is anything other than capital which the owner of the land is receiving?

I should like to say only a word on the same subject. I do not know whether the committee is clear as to the exact meaning of a royalty. Perhaps I might put it this way. We will say that a man owns a quarter-section of land and the oil underneath it. This question is of particular interest to the Leduc area because it is one of the oldest settled areas in Alberta. When the government of Canada granted land titles, the grants included the rights to mines and minerals-and oil has been held to be a mineral. A man owns the oil just as much as someone in Ottawa may own a building; there is no difference in principle. Oil may be found in a neighbourhood, following which an oil company will come along and buy the oil under the land. But the company will buy only, we will say, seven-eighths of it. In this instance I am speaking only for the small group of farmers who own the oil rights under their land. The oil company will make a development, with the farmer still owning one-eighth.
Let us assume that across the river in Hull I have some huge tanks containing 100,000 barrels of oil. It may be that I have no sale for it in Hull, or that it commands a better sale in Ottawa. I move my 100,000 barrels of oil to Ottawa so that I can sell it here. Obviously no tax would be involved. Exactly the same reasoning applies to oil under the ground. Instead of moving the oil horizontally, as in the illustration I have given, I move vertically the oil which is under the ground. That is the only difference in principle, legally or otherwise, that can possibly be attached to this question of royalties.
It is said that certain allowances are made. I know that; and I have no objection to them. But this is a tax on capital, and it is nothing else. You do not need to worry about the companies who develop the oil. That is their business, and so they pay taxes.
I am not speaking for them at all. I am speaking for the individual farmer who owns this land and has oil as part of his land.
Let us assume that down here a few years ago I bought a thousand shares of Consolidated. That is an imaginary purchase, of course, because I never had enough money to buy a thousand shares of Consolidated. Then suppose that after holding those shares for some time I sell them at present prices. I have made a capital gain. I owned some oil,

Incovie Tax Act
it increased greatly in value, and I sold it. I have done nothing more than make a capital gain. Remember I am not in the oil business; I am a farmer and I am still farming the surface of my land.
Let me give another illustration-and this actually happened. The owner of a quarter-section of land is permitted under government regulations to drill four wells. In the case I have in mind the farmer, or his solicitor when he sold seven-eighths to the oil company very foolishly put in a clause providing that the company must develop those wells consecutively and without delay. He has four wells operating on that property. The four wells bring in daily a lot of oil. They are limited to 175 barrels a day-to take a round figure we will say 200 barrels. That farmer has, then, 800 barrels a day coming in. That will sell for approximately S3 a barrel, or $2,400. One-eighth of that is S300, and according to the present ruling he would pay income tax on the total $300. A mile away, we will say, is another man who has sold his land. They get cash, of course, as much as $200,000 for a quarter section. He has made his sale, but his sale agreement does not contain this quick development clause, and so the company drills one well on his property and then goes and looks after its business elsewhere. The result is that that man pays this year only on the product of that one well, whereas his neighbour is paying taxes on the four producing wells. The man who had the quick-drilling clause in his agreement is in a bracket away beyond the chap a mile away *who has only one well producing. The law works an extreme injustice as between those two persons. I want to make this plain: I am talking of actual cases. I know of cases which parallel the illustrations I am giving.
I would like very much to have someone tell me, first of all, why this capital gain is taxable, and next, whether something cannot be done to level off as between the two farmers about whom I have been speaking.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have followed my hon. friend closely. It is a technical subject, and I have not, of course, his knowledge of the practical operations, and certainly not of the way in which these contracts are drawn. But this is a question of policy. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, I appreciated later, was speaking not of the drafting of the act but of the policy. I am told that this has been the policy since 1934, and all I can say now is that I will study the question that has been raised by the hon. member for Calgary West, and see what, if anything, can be done. It 5849-362
would be a matter that would have to be taken care of as a budgetary item and not by revision through this bill.

I suppose I must be content with what the minister has said, but he will remember what happened in the Spooner case, which went to the privy council. The privy council held that this was a capital asset, and then the government for reasons best known to itself passed a statute which said it is not a capital asset. That, in laymen's language, is what happened. The main point I have in mind is this, apart altogether from the individuals who will be called upon to pay these tremendous taxes. This policy is a departure from the over-all principle of our taxation, because we in Canada have not yet seen fit, as they have to some extent in the United States, to tax capital gains, and why we should pick out these poor farmers-they were poor; they are not now-and tax their capital gains while we do not tax the capital gains of well-off people who bu3r stocks and shares, is something I cannot understand. The farmer who has been working on his farm for perhaps thirty or forty years has his capital gains taxed. That may be a matter of government policy. If it is, it is a kind of government policy which someone should be prepared to justify.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will certainly look into it. The change was made when Mr. Bennett was prime minister. Perhaps he knew more about oil than I do. At any rate I will look into it.
May I answer the remark that the change was made when Mr. Bennett was prime minister? It was made by the same officials in your department who were there when Mr. Bennett was there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think any officials made Mr. Bennett's decisions for him, did they?
It is possible for anyone, including Mr. Bennett, to make a mistake.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I know it is a favourite sport to blame things on officials. I find people all too prone to blame their own shortcomings on officials.

There is a kindred question which I think might be considered by the minister when he is considering the matters raised by the hon. members for Calgary West and Muskoka-Ontario. I refer to the allowance made for depletion. Twenty per cent is allowed on dividends from Canadian wells, and only ten per cent on dividends from wells situated elsewhere, principally in the United States.
Income Tax Act

The argument has been advanced that governments can supervise more effectively the accountancy and methods of operation of Canadian companies than they can of United States companies. With the treaty arrangements which exist between the United States and this country, that is not altogther a satisfactory answer. Moreover, the same principle does not apply to mines. The department allow certain depletion with regard to mines in Canada, and if my information be correct they allow the same depletion with regard to mines outside of Canada, particularly in the United States. As the act is being revised, it would seem well to endeavour to introduce more uniformity and equity into its terms.

I am sure the minister realized that I was pinch-hitting for the hon. member for Calgary West. I do not need to tell him that. I do want to add this one thing. This taxation is in essence a kind of punitive taxation. It appears to be the result of the feeling that here is somebody who has something of which he may be despoiled, and we can do it. When the minister is thinking this over I suggest very earnestly that it is not a good basis of taxation. If capital gain should be taxed, for which there is an argument, all right, tax it; but I think it is undesirable to pick out one and leave the others alone.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

On section 9

Winding-up.

Subsection 3 says that in the case of reorganization or readjustment of the capital stock the new shares shall be taxable in the hands of the shareholder to the extent that any unearned surplus is used to make up the capitalization or the new stated value of the shares. I think that is a fair enough provision so far as it affects Canadian companies, where the earned surplus would ordinarily be taxable when paid out. But it causes a considerable amount of embarrassment and confusion to Canadian shareholders of the United States corporations which subdivide their shares and allocate a part of their United States earned surplus, which would in

no case be taxable by our own government when they issue the new subdivided shares. For that reason I feel that there should be some limitation in subsection 3 so that a Canadian shareholder in the position I have outlined would know what his taxation status was, and that the best thing for him to do would be to dispose of his United States shares and thereby lose opportunities to benefit himself and the whole Canadian economy.
If the United States company is subdividing its shares it is not very likely to consider the distribution of more than all its earned surplus. On the other hand, it will likely be distributing its current earnings, and the shareholder here would not benefit from the earned surplus that is not to be distributed. The company is obviously in a profitable condition if it is subdividing its shares. I do not think the government would lose any revenue, but on the other hand it would simplify the holding of United States shares by Canadians and allow them to stay in a situation which had proven profitable, and which would continue to prove profitable, and thereby make greater income in their hands available to the taxing authorities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps I may say a word in reference to what the hon. member for Rose-dale said. I am aware of the problem that he has put forward. It is a complex one, and there are serious administrative difficulties. Among other things it must be shown that there is undistributed income in the hands of the United States company which renders the Canadian shareholder liable to taxes on the reorganization. I am told that in some cases the financial structure is so complex that it has been far from clear that there was any tax liability. We are aware of the problem. We have not been able to devise any limitation which can be put in here which would be sufficiently general to make it administratively possible to handle' the section.
Why is it not possible simply to limit this section to subdivision of shares on the part of the Canadian company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We would lose taxes on something which is properly income and which we should get. That is the difficulty there.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
There is an amendment to paragraph (b) of subsection 1 of section 11. The amendment reads:
Such amount as an allowance in respect of an oil or gas well, mine or timber limit, if any, as is allowed to the taxpayer by regulation.

Income Tax Act
The minister no doubt has had a letter from the professional engineers asking whether their expenses could be deducted from their income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. I have not only had a letter but I have had a delegation from the professional engineers. This question as to what is deductible from wages and salaries has been before the committee a great many times. If the engineer is engaged on a fee basis and has a gross income, he of course deducts his expenses; but the representation to which my hon. friend referred related to engineers who are employed on a salary by corporations and others. As the committee knows, there are no deductions from salaries for expenses. That has to apply to engineers the same as it does to others, but I have had the representations to which the hon. member referred. It really should come under section 5, although it may be brought up here.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
There is a further amendment to section 11. The amendment refers to subsection 2 on page 9 of the bill. As amended it will read1 as follows:
There may be deducted in computing the income of a shareholder from shares in a corporation whose income is from the operation of an oil or gas well, or mine, such amount, if any, as is allowed by regulation.
Then, subsection 3 will read:
Where a deduction is allowed under paragraph (b) of section 1 in respect of oil or gas well, mine or timber limited operated by a lessee, the lessor and lessee may agree as to what portion of the allowance each may deduct and, in the event that they cannot agree, the minister may fix the portions.

I -want to put forward briefly a point which was raised with respect to paragraph (g) of subsection 1 of section 11, having to do with deductions from income for contributions to superannuation funds. Since this matter was raised in the committee I have had a number of further representations to the effect that while this deduction is applied to those who contribute to approved superannuation or pension funds, no provision is made for those who arrange their own retirement by way of insurance premiums or annuity policies, and that fact works a grave hardship. The suggestion made, that the minister take this into consideration and revise it if possible at the next budget, seems to have met with a degree of favourable approval in the committee. I would ask the minister to. repeat the assurance, if he can, and say whether in the meantime he has given further thought to the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have not been able to give further thought to this particular question, but I did assure the members of the banking and
commerce committee that these sections relating to deductions for pension schemes and the like would be thoroughly reviewed before the presentation of the next budget.

May I raise one other question? I have had letters from persons employed in an industry in central Ontario seeking information as to why the government is charging income tax on cost of living bonuses. Apparently these cost of living bonuses fluctuate in certain plants. If the cost of living goes down, the bonus disappears, but when the cost of living goes up, a compensating factor is provided by the additional amount. I am not an expert on income tax, and I think that remark applies to many hon. members in this house. Perhaps it is because we have not had enough income to become really experienced in it. In any event, can the minister enlighten me, as one of the inexperienced laymen so far as this subject is concerned, just what this all means, and what the possibilities are of giving these people the relief for which they are asking?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not familiar with the exact form which this cost of living bonus takes, but I suppose it is an increase in salaries or wages depending upon the increase in the cost of living index. It is true it is expected that it will take care of the increased cost of living, but that applies to other wage increases, whether tied to the cost of living index or not, and the general principle of the income tax law, as hon. members know, is that income is taxed. After all, broadly speaking, one's whole income is intended to enable one to meet the cost of living. For that reason no consideration has ever been given to establishing a tax exemption on earnings. As to expenses, these are deducted from gross income as allowed under the law before arriving at net income.. I do not think it would be possible, and certainly it would not be consistent with the income tax structure, to permit this form of wage or salary increase to be exempt from income tax. That is the principle on which the law has proceeded.

There are several questions I wish to ask and perhaps the minister can answer them all at the same time.
I would like to know whether the regulations when they are made will be published, and also why parliament should not be asked to approve of such regulations.
I would like to know why the sum of $900 has been fixed as the maximum for contributions to pension funds, whether or not a larger percentage should be allowed, perhaps to the man in the lower brackets, and to what extent
Income Tax Act

it will help him as against loss to the public as a whole of its revenue.
I come now to clause (j), which refers to the amount allowed to the taxpayer who is separated from his wife. I think the converse applies when the wife separates from her husband. I would like to know whether or not this puts the taxpayer who is separated from his wife in a preferred position in the matter of income tax. As I understand it, most of us are allowed S750 as exemption on account of having a wife, which is not always sufficient to meet what we actually spend for her; yet if a man is separated from his wife he is allowed an expenditure of perhaps $2,000 or $3,000 if his payments amount to that much. The maximum should be $750. I will admit that the wife is taxed also, but as to those in the lower income tax brackets, the wife might have little other income and she would be in a preferred position.
Then we come to subsection 5(a), the capital cost of property. Again I would like to know what the capital cost of property is. How is it arrived at? I believe that in some -cases property when transferred, having been depreciated once, starts once again on the 'long road of depreciation for the new owner. I would like to know how the department intends to arrive at the capital cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
First as to the question of regulations, my hon, friend was not in the [DOT]committee when I explained that in the revision we have tried to eliminate as many *of the ministerial discretions as possible. I expressed the view that perhaps we had eliminated too many, and we may have to put some back, because most of them were put in to enable the rigorous provisions of the act to be relaxed. In any event, that will be demonstrated by the process of trial and error. The principle followed, where it is obviously necessary to leave some measure of flexibility in the act, and it is not possible to spell out every single case, is to provide that they may be covered by regulation to be adopted by the governor in council in the form of order in council, to be published. I would expect that these regulations would form a volume which would be available to all taxpayers, and to lawyers and accountants for the purpose of enabling them to inform themselves and to advise their clients.
The regulations under this act have not yet been prepared. They are being worked on, but the act is not to come into force until the first of January next, and well before that time we expect to have the regulations adopted. I would hope that well in advance of the first of January they will be published

so that they can be subject to examination and criticism by those interested. That is the reason for the regulations.
I do not recall why $900 was selected as the amount which may be deducted from earnings as contribution to an approved pension plan. It represents $75 a month, and six per cent interest on $15,000. But one has to take a figure somewhere, and that figure was selected some time ago. There is no change in the law here.
As regards the question of alimony, it is some little time since I piloted this resolution through the house, and since I have never been personally interested, the relevant considerations have escaped me at the moment. I think it is fair, however. It was introduced first for one year and representations were made that it was too rigorous and an amendment was made in the following year to make it permanent. That is my recollection.
There was nothing left after the two taxes were imposed. It created a hardship which was impossible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the hon. member is right. The change was made after the other tax was imposed. The last question asked by the hon. member was: What is capital cost of the property, in subsection 5? I am informed that it is what the taxpayer paid for it.

In regard to subsection 8 of section 11, which has to do with expenses of transport employees, a good many railway workers, the running trades in particular, complain that the amount allowed for deduction from income tax on account of expenses while working away from home is inadequate. They point out that the cost of living has gone up substantially in hotels and rooming houses, and of course the cost of meals has increased 4-0 per cent. I think the general consensus amongst these workers is that there should be an increase of at least 33J per cent in this exemption.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is no requirement for any increase. They are allowed their actual expenses for board and room while away from home. It may be that some of the brotherhoods have an arrangement with the Department of National Revenue under which a standard rate is taken; I do not know. But that is an administrative matter. A member of the running trades is entitled to claim his actual out-of-pocket expenses for board and room. Of course they must be reasonable. I do not suppose he would be allowed to take a suite at the Chateau Laurier-I am saying that in a joking way, of course. But the law

Income Tax Act

enables him to claim his actual expenses for board and room when away from home.
I think this section is giving reasonable satisfaction to the trades, and it is being extended to other transport workers.
Is this changed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not changed. There was a budget item extending the operation of this clause. There is no change in this bill.

I asked the minister when the bill was before the house if he would give certain detailed information as to the tax imposed by the state of New York, as to the number of states in the union which bad higher income taxes than New York and the number which had lower income taxes. It seems to me that this may be an opportune moment for him to give that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have that information, Mr. Chairman, but I left it in my office. I thought I had it among my papers here. I can send for it and have it in a few minutes.
If the minister will get it and bring it forward at some conveniently early moment, I shall be satisfied.

As to the question brought up by the hon. member for Kamloops, allowance for insurance payments, may I ask if such an allowance is not made under the British income tax act? People over there are allowed a deduction for insurance premiums, are they not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think I was told there was some deduction. I am not quite sure. I would have to verify that. I am going to look into the whole situation, anyway.

The minister made a statement with respect to the running trades on the railroads. He said jokingly that he did not suppose they would be permitted to have a suite at the Chateau Laurier, but the fact remains that if they have a suite at the Chateau Laurier and can prove that they spent their money living in that place, they are entitled to that exemption. They submit their bills to prove they actually paid the money out. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. They would not be able to do that, because under section 12, subsection 2, no one is entitled to deduct, in computing income, anything except in respect of an outlay or expense which was reasonable in the circumstances. I do not think it would be considered reasonable that, let us say, a conductor or an engineer who in the course of his duties had to stay overnight in Ottawa should take a suite at the Chateau Laurier. Perhaps
I should not have used that example; I said it jokingly. It is quite clear that that would not be allowed. It must be a reasonable expense.

That is all right. What I wanted to get at was this. If he can submit bona fide vouchers that he has paid out a certain amount of money, and it is a reasonable expense- we will use that word-he is entitled to that exemption?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is quite correct.

I was not in the committee at the beginning, but can the minister tell me if his attention has been called to the fact that in the preamble the word "may" in the second line might be changed to "shall"?

speechtext: Which section is my hon. friend referring to?
Section 11, subsection 1. The tax foundation have criticized this preamble in that it does not say "shall".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told by the assistant deputy minister that "may" is the correct word. It is permissive. It does not require him to give a reduction unless he wishes to do so.
The point is that the taxpayer should be protected by a stronger clause, and they have suggested "shall be entitled to deduct."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is what "may" means. It is the old argument of the lawyers as to the correct use of "may" and "shall". I think it is all right, Mr. Chairman. It has been this way for a long time.
I have just come in from another committee. With regard to section 11, may I ask if the amendments which were made in the banking and commerce committee have been incorporated in the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All the amendments have been incorporated in the bill which was before the committee.

On section 12-Deductions not allowed in computing income.

Section 12 has been criticized' on the ground that it-
. . . excludes many ordinary and proper business expenses resulting in a necessary exercise of administrative discretion going beyond the law and causing uncertainty for the taxpayer.
Has the minister's attention been called to that criticism?

Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not aware of that criticism. This section-with others, of course 

has been the subject of representations from all sorts of representative groups such as boards of trade, the tax foundation, the chartered accountants association, the Canadian Bar Association, and others. There is, if anything, a relaxation of the present wording by this section. It has always, however, been the law in some form.

The tax foundation have
recommended that the wording be changed to something of this type:
No deduction shall be permitted in respect of any item of any item of expenditure or of charge except so far as it is attributable to and incurred for the purposes of the business.
That is the wording proposed by the British codification committee, 1936. They felt that would be an improvement to this section and would protect the businessman to a considerable extent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

A good many people have different sources of income. For instance one member the other day who, in addition to being a member of parliament, is also a successful farmer, asked if he could charge the losses on his farm against his indemnity as a member of parliament. The rule is that if an individual has a secondary source of income -or to be more specific, if my principal occupation is that of a cabinet minister but I operate a farm on the side, I cannot charge my farm expenses, in the event of my making a loss on my farming operations, against my salary as a cabinet minister. Secondary income can be charged only with the expenses incurred in connection with the earning of that secondary income.
Sometimes it is difficult to determine a man's principal occupation for taxation purposes, as against his secondary occupation. It was for that reason that it was felt by many that the only way to resolve the question was to place the discretion in the hands of the minister, in the interests of the taxpayer. That has been done, and I believe I have given the explanation for it.

I want to raise one point for the minister's consideration. I take it that it is fair to say that clause 21 in a sense disregards entirely t'he conception of the English law with regard to the position of a wife holding property and so on. I do not know whether the minister is at all affected by the conception of the law of the province in which he lives, under which the relations between husband and wife in this regard are very different. I remember when I first went to live in Quebec it seemed a good idea that a husband could not give a present to his wife, but I discovered later that that was not as alluring as it seemed to be.
Considered and careful recommendations have been made on this question by the Canadian Tax Foundation. The minister is familiar with them and I do not need to labour the point. But I do ask him this question: Why is it that none of the recommendations from this reputable source have been given effect to? I think the minister will agree that the recommendations of the Canadian Tax Foundation recognize the full legal status of

women, even when married, and at the same time their recommendations would prevent anything in the nature of fraud or colourable transactions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will have a look at their recommendations again. For the moment they have gone out of my head. The principle of this section is very simple. There is nothing to prevent husband and wife from making transfers one to the other if they care to do so, and if it is legal to do so in the jurisdiction in which they live, but these transfers are not permitted to affect the relative income tax liability of the consorts. That is the purpose of the section. It does not seem to me that there is anything objectionable in its terms. Subsection 2 relates to one of the consorts being employed by the other. That is a principle which has been in the law for a long time.

I should like to put on the record one of the recommendations of the Canadian Tax Foundation with respect to clause 21. I will first read the clause as it stands:
Where a person has, on or after the first day of August, 1947, transferred property, either directly or indirectly, by means of a trust or by any other means whatsoever, to his spouse, or to a person who has since become his spouse, the income for a taxation year from the property or from property substituted therefor shall be deemed to be income of the transferor and not of the transferee.
Their recommendation is to insert after the word "spouse", where it first occurs, the words "and not for a consideration reasonably corresponding to the fair value of the property so transferred". As the section reads in the bill, a husband is not allowed to enter into a transaction of any kind with his wife, even though she has her own property, and the purpose of the amendment proposed by the Canadian Tax Foundation is to head off any colourable or fictitious transaction. In other words, what this organization recommends is that it should be possible for ordinary business transactions to take place between husband and wife, provided it is clear that they are proper business transactions and not a frame-up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will look at the brief he will see that it says a little further on:
The recommendations are self-explanatory. It was realized that the administrative problem is formidable, but agreed that the taxpayer should be adequately protected in bona fide situations.
Where do we stop? A good many transfers are made for love and affection, and that is a

So far as husband and wife are concerned, where a close relationship exists between them, it is not unreasonable that transfers between them should not affect the tax position of the transferor. That is the view which the law has taken for a good many years, and I would be most reluctant to make a change in policy of that kind.

It seems to me that this is a far-reaching section. I should like the committee to listen to the few lines which are found in subsection 1, which read as follows:
Where a person has, on or after the first day of August, 1917, transferred property, either directly or indirectly, by means of a trust or by any other means whatsoever, to his spouse, or to a person who has since become his spouse, the income for a taxation year from the property or from property substituted therefor shall be deemed to be income of the transferor and not of the transferee.
Is there some other subsection which mitigates the absoluteness, of that rule?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not that I am aware of.

Let us take this case, and it is not one which wall make any heav37 demand upon the imagination. A young man becomes engaged to a young woman and they enter into a marriage contract. That is a very ordinary transaction in the jurisdiction with which the Minister of Finance is familiar. By the terms of that document the young man confers upon the spouse a benefit of $50,000. If he has the money he can give it to her at that time, and I understand that under this section the revenue from it wall be taxable revenue in the hands of the husband for ever. Or, being penniless at the time, he may, having made this gift, pay it at a future time.
I cannot speak for the law in other provinces, but that is one of the few exceptions which the law of the province of Quebec makes as regards benefits between spouses. That young man may make a gift of future property to his spouse-to-be, and if fortune smile upon him he may make this payment in the future. When the undertaking is implemented, the property transferred becomes the absolute property of the spouse. Unless there be in the act some provision which I have not yet discovered- and I understood from the minister that there was nothing to mitigate the harshness of the section I have read-it will no longer be possible for a future husband, or a person who is about to become a husband, to make a transfer of property in favour of his future wife which will free him from the obligation of paying income tax on any revenue that may be derived from the capital transferred.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that there is much comment I can make, other than that this is a provision which has been in the law for a great many years. My hon. friend has said that I am familiar with the provisions, which relate to the jurisdiction from which we both come, that gifts are made in contemplation of marriage. Whether it prevails in other jurisdictions, I do not know'. I have no doubt it does, but perhaps not to the same extent as it does in Quebec. The law provides that as between the two consorts these gifts shall not affect the income tax position of the person who makes the gift, and that for income tax purposes, and income tax purposes only, the revenues of the property transferred, or to be transferred, will be considered as the income of the transferor. One could argue, I suppose, that that provision should be changed, and that is what my hon. friend is doing; but I must again say it seems to me that if that short of change were to be made it is one which should be a budgetary provision and made as a distinct departure from the existing law7.

Subsection 2 of section 21 deals with the case of a spouse who is an employee of the husband or wife, as the case may be. It provides that the remuneration or salary paid to that employee cannot be deducted from the income tax of the business. The Canadian Tax Foundation suggested that there be added to the end of the subsection these words:
But this subsection shall not apply cvhere the employee spouse is a bona fide employee, is paid at the prevailing wage rates and actively fills a position necessary in the business.
The suggested amendment does seem to be reasonable. Would it not be possible to have it added to subsection 2?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That recommendation was carefully and extensively considered. I think it will be apparent to hon. members that it imposes a difficult test for the tax administration to determine, as the tax foundation said in their submission. They realized that 'it imposed extremely difficult administrative problems.
Again, this is a rule which has been in the law for a great many years. Whether it goes back to the origin of the law in 1917 or 191S I cannot say offhand, but it has been

the rule. The recommendation was considered, but it was felt that it would be administratively impossible to enforce without the risk of grave abuses.

speechtext: But at a very different rate. The obvious thing is that it would be an easy way for the husband and wife to divide their income and thereby get into the lower bracket.

I had not quite finished.
I beg to differ from the minister when he states that subsection 1 of section 21 has been in the act from its inception or for a long time. The bill indicates that subsection 1 of section 21 replaces subsection 2 of section 32. Subsection 2 of section 32 is in these terms:
Where a husband transfers property to his wife, or vice versa, the husband or the wife, as the case may be, shall nevertheless be liable to be taxed on the income derived from such property or from properties substituted therefor as if such transfer had not been made.
I am going to point out some of the differences between the bill and the old law. In the first place, the old law is not retroactive. This subsection enables the tax collector to go back some thirty-one years and compel an individual who had transferred property to a person who later became his wife to pay income tax on benefits which his wife had legally and properly received and possibly paid income tax on for thirty odd years. With great deference I submit that the enactment of such legislation is nothing less than tyrannous and is something heretofore entirely unknown to this legislative body.
In the second place, I point out that the law as it stood did not apply to contracts between persons who were about to become man and wife. Any contract entered into which favoured the founding of a home and the protection of the family has always had the approval of the legislature. But here we find that even persons entering into the bonds of matrimony may not, as regards taxation and income tax, make any arrangements with regard to the future. That is to say, it is no longer possible for one of the contracting parties before marriage, and in aniticipation of the burdens and uncertainties of marriage, to make any provision for the future of the other, and to that extent I do not hesitate to say that this law is against the welfare of the family. It is anti-social and amazing in its harshness.
IMr. Abbott.]
Furthermore, I would point out to the minister that when lie spoke of this act on April 29, 1947, as reported at page 2557 of Hansard, he said that the new act was merely a recodification and would contain no new law. That is the substance and significance of his words. He said:
I am endeavouring to make this a relatively simple budget and I am not, therefore, proposing any other substantial changes at this time in the income tax, although I shall later mention some minor amendments. We have been busy during the past year upon the rewriting of our basic income tax law in an effort to improve its arrangement, to make it clearer and simpler, and to remove ambiguities and anomalies. Hon. members will, I think, be particularly pleased with the extent to which it will be less dependent upon the exercise of ministerial discretions-
And so forth. If that undertaking meant anything it meant that there would be no substantial or radical changes in the act. This is a radical, far-reaching change, a change that goes to the very foundation of the home, and I am going to move, seconded by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdon-nell), that section 21 (1) be struck from the bill and replaced by the section in the act as it now stands, 32 (2).
Before I sit down I would like to say a word to my colleagues from the province of Quebec. I ask them whether they are aware, whether they fully realize, that this is an invasion upon a right which they have cherished and for which they have stood and will stand, I believe, despite these unconsidered and antisocial amendments.
If there is one place in Canada where the integrity of the family has withstood the onslaught of modern phases and fancies it is in the province of Quebec, and I shall be astonished if the members from that province, having considered the full meaning and purport of this bill, will give their support to it when it is a direct undermining influence upon that greatest of institutions, the home.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have been greatly impressed and moved by the appeal which the hon. member for Stanstead has made as to the sanctity of the home. I say to him that I am just as jealous of the traditions and1 the laws of the province of Quebec as he is, but I say to him also that this is not making any changes in the laws of the province of Quebec. It is essential that a person who makes a marriage contract, whether in the province of Quebec or anywhere else, shall not, by transferring from wife to husband or from husband to wife, get income tax advantage which another taxpayer cannot get.
That is all that this section does, and it is not aimed particularly at Quebec or any other

Income Tax Act
province. It is intended to provide that these interconjugal transfers, if I may so describe them, will not affect the income tax position of consorts. That is all this section is intended to do. It is intended to ensure that the man who is smart enough to make a contract whereby he reserves to himself the right to transfer to his wife $25,000, $50,000 or $100,000, which he has not today, but when he gets it, shall not get income tax advantage by making that contract. That is all the section is intended to do. It is not attacking the sanctity of the home or the laws of the province of Quebec. It is not attacking anything. It is intended to ensure that every taxpayer shall pay his fair share of taxes. I do not think I can make it any clearer.

The section seems to assume that a person has transferred property to his spouse, or to a person who has since become his spouse. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I do not know that it has ever arisen, and perhaps I should not give an opinion. The Secretary of State for External Affairs and I were discussing it. In most jurisdictions there is no prohibition against a contract of sale between a husband and wife. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The election is almost over in Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Well, here is one place where the Minister of Finance, with that open mind of his, could make a change which would be acceptable by those in his own party, who are interested and which would mean something to the people at large. It is hard to know what figure to suggest now, because the cost of living keeps going up. But surely this exemption level ought not to be lower than $1,200 for a single person and $2,000 or perhaps $2,400 for a married person.
If I did not know it from the discussion which took place a few moments ago, then I would know from the rules of the house that any attempt on the part of a private member to move an amendment to change these figures would be ruled out of order. After all, to raise the exemption level would change the amount of income available to the government. I might, of course, propose as an alternative a reimposition of the excess profits tax, but that might be difficult to win in this house. I do suggest however that we ought not to ride over this section too quickly. It is not improper for the committee to take a bit of time to discuss the matter. It would not be out of the way for members from all groups on this side of the house, and those on the government side, to let the government know that a change in these exemption levels is highly desirable. It does not meet the whole of the problem; something has to be done about the cost of living. But it would be a help if the exemption levels were brought up to some figure consonant with what it costs to maintain a decent standard of living at the present time.
I hope the minister will not stand on ceremony; I hope he will not insist that no major change can be made at the present time. He

has the authority. He has often told us that he was not engaged in any popularity contest so far as his taxation measures are concerned. Here is a chance to regain some of the popularity he has lo^t by making a worthwhile step at this closing period of the session. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not suppose I need to urge hon. members on all sides of the house to make speeches asking for increases in exemption levels. I am quite sure everyone would be pleased if it were possible to do so. I should be pleased myself. But in the course of the budget debate and at other times I have had occasion to give the reasons why I do not think that very important policy move can be made this year. The exemption levels in Canada, as I have had occasion to reiterate on a number of occasions, are already higher -much higher-than they are in the United Kingdom, and the United States. I hope at some time it may be possible to increase them, but I also hope that all members who are in sympathy with that very desirable objective will not feel called upon to urge it now. I am sure all hon. members are as much interested in that as is the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

I shall not raise any argument which will disturb the balance of ways and means. I do believe, however, that there are administrative details in the act which could be cleared up. I have had correspondence with the department on two or three matters which seem to be sore spots.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made a general statement on the subject with which we all agree. I do not think, however, from the minister's statement that there will be any change.
There are two or three points I would bring to the minister's attention. First of all, $300 a year for purposes of income tax are added to the salaries of sleeping car porters, on the basis of the assumption that they receive that amount of money per year in tips. Whether they get that much or not, they are taxed on an extra $300. They may make it on some sections of road, but there are other sections where sleeping-car porters do not take in $300 in tips. I believe that is a wrong principle. First it encourages the railway company to pay low wages. Furthermore, it is not fair to sleeping-car porters who may not receive that much in tips.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A porter may keep a record and put in his actual receipts.

Even so, I think it is unfair. If a porter does a good job which requires his working longer hours, shining shoes and all that kind of thing, a passenger who wishes to give him a dollar or two should be permitted to do so without making it necessary for him to declare it as income. If it is desired to tax that extra amount, then the railway companies should be told to pay larger salaries so that the government could get it back in the regular way. This would be an administrative change.
My next point has to do with the exemption for a boy or a girl in university until he or she reaches the age of twenty-one. After that age is passed the student is no longer considered as a dependent for income tax purposes. The period ought to be extended until the student graduates. In may instances parents are having great difficulty in putting young people through university. Perhaps a student will reach the age of twenty-one before his last year at school. That is the most expensive year, and that is the time when the student is cut off as a dependent, with the hardship which stems from that situation.
I suggest that the regulations be changed so that the age be placed beyond twenty-one years, and that it apply until graduation. If the provision is necessary in early years of university training, it continues to be necessary until the day of graduation.
I wish to discuss also the matter of exemption for wives and husbands both of whom are employed. Rather than make a speech on the subject I shall read a paragraph from a letter I have received, which I would ask the minister to consider carefully. We hear a good deal of talk about the sanctity of the home. I believe the present arrangement respecting husbands and wives who have taxable incomes is creating a complication in the minds of people, one which leads them to think that it is much better to pick up a girl, live with her and not marry her. because in that way one can save money. On this matter of the sanctity of the home, it surprises me, when there are so many gentlemen of the cloth in the chamber, that they have not been waving their arms about the matter for a long time.
The letter states in part:
A single man and woman both earning in excess of $750 each, living together, unwedded, with one child or dependent, can receive an exemption of $2,250. Here is how: he files an income tax form, for himself and child which gives him married status with an exemption of $1,500; woman files one for herself for an exemption of $750. But the married man whose Wife earns $750 files a form for himself and child, single status $850, wife's form $750, total
Income Tax Act

$1,600. I verified the above exemptions at our district income tax office. They could not give an explanation, but said that according to income tax form T-l Special, that was how it stood. And moreover the unwedded couple are allowed exemptions for a housekeeper, yet the married couple are not, even though it is an absolute necessity if both are to work. Now in view of the above facts anyone can see that the married man is not getting a single man's status. He is paying $129 more in income tax than the single man; if he wants single status man and wife have to live apart. He will then save $129 and the government will not receive a cent more from her.
That is how the exemptions work out. I think it is due to an oversight. I suggest that the minister set one of his experts to work and at least even this thing up, because as things stand it is completely wrong. I have discussed it with some of the district officials and they cannot account for it. I suggest that the minister take it into consideration and do something about it.
