ing one's ills, and so forth. I do not see anything in this clause to provide that payments made to that profession on account of one's health may be deducted as medical expenses. Is there any reason why that should not be included?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The language of the act is medical practitioners. I do not know what stand the Department of National Revenue has taken administratively as to whether chiropractors are recognized as coming within that description or not.
They do not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend says they do not.

I wonder why. I am not offering an amendment. I suggest that consideration be given to that, because I know of people- as a matter of fact I have had a little experience myself-who have found that profession more helpful to them than the medical practitioners in certain circumstances. They should be able to obtain the benefit of the deductions for those expenses as they would be for expenses to a medical practitioner.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a matter of interpretation of the phrase "medical practitioner". I understand that the Department of National Revenue has not included chiropractors in that interpretation. Of course it would be open to the courts to take a different view if the matter were brought before them.

May I return to a discussion of the medical side of it? It has come to my attention that sufferers from diabetes, who must necessarily have insulin injections, are not able to make any deduction from their income tax for the constant expense of insulin which they must buy, either through their doctor or from the druggist. In chronic illnesses such as these, it seems to me that the government should give some consideration to people who must necessarily make a continuing expenditure of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: 1 shall look into that, because I can see that it would be a special type of case.

After the committee hearings, did the minister give any consideration to making the four per cent of the taxpayer's income read four per cent of the taxpayer's income after taxation? It makes quite a difference. I noticed, further on, that there is a limitation of $1,000 in any case; therefore I do not think it would ever injure the treasury. It would foe a factor and it would be merciful in certain cases, particularly in view of the fact

Income Tax Act
that the person with the large gross income does pay in doctor's fees, particularly for operations,'a substantial part of the cost of the public wards, and so forth.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did give consideration to that. My hon. friend raised it in committee.
I must say I do not feel that we should make that distinction. I may be wrong; but in any event I came to that conclusion. Of course it would be obviously advantageous to the man with the larger gross income.
Advantageous to everybody.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Suppose a man goes to Rochester for an operation which costs him 82,000. Is there any provision to take care of that cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. He can claim 82,000 as a deduction from his income to the extent to which it is in excess of four per cent of his income. Four per cent is regarded as the average, and anything in excess of that can be claimed as a deduction. It used to be five per cent and was reduced to four per cent. It was originally five per cent, the extra one per cent being allowed to cover such things as drugs.

Mr. Chairman, may I suggest that hon. members who wish to speak address the Chair, and speak in a voice loud enough for the rest of us to hear them. Members sitting near the minister mumble and we do not know what they are saying.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
That is a good idea. As Chairman I wish to bring one point to the attention of the committee. This discussion has been general, and while it was taking place I looked up the resolution on which the bill was based. The resolution was passed on June 4, on which date the Minister of Finance moved that the house go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to revise and consolidate the law respecting the levying of income tax and the administration thereof.
The committee is bound by the terms of the resolution, and hon. members will notice that the only power is to revise and consolidate the law. It occurred to me, therefore, that it would be beyond the power of the committee to make any substantial change in the law. I do not think it would be permissible to have another discussion at this time on the fiscal policy of the government. That discussion took place when the budget resolutions were before the house and the committee. Shall the section carry?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 27-Dividends received by a corporation.

This clause deals with "business losses", (26) (d). When I was home recently a case was brought to my attention of a business having been closed and put up for sale by the sheriff. The proceeds were about to be distributed, and seven days before the distribution was to take place the income tax branch notified the sheriff that there was an account owing for income tax two years previously, and instructed him not to make the distribution. These are the facts as they came to me. In Nova Scotia and in other provinces, workmens liens are given priority; and in this case, if the income tax branch has its way, no payment would be made to the workmen from the proceeds of the sheriff's sale because the income tax branch claims the full amount. That would be a great injustice to these workmen. They worked for some months prior to the projected sale, and they would be denied pay for their labour. If the minister cannot answrer the question now, I would ask him to do -what he has promised to do in other cases, namely, to look into the matter to see whether there is not an injustice as far as these workmen are concerned, and that he give instructions to the department in Halifax, so that the men get their priority for wages, as should be their right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be glad to look into the situation. It relates to the Halifax office?
Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Sections 28 to 44 inclusive agreed to.
On section 45-Farmers.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There is an amendment in the second line of the clause, which will now read:
Every individual whose chief source of income is farming or fishing . . .
Is any effort being made to simplify the form for farmers' income tax returns?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am assured that the officials are working day and night on it.

It does not come under the minister's jurisdiction?
Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is under National
Revenue, but one of the senior officers in front of me assures me that they are working at it.
I suggest that the officials could save themselves a good deal of time by greatly simplifying the forms, instead of putting so much work on them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is what they are trying to do.

I hope they eliminate three-quarters of the questions. This section provides that on or before December 31 in each taxation year the taxpayer shall pay two-thirds of the tax as estimated by him at the rates for the year on his estimated taxable income for the year, or on his taxable income for the immediately preceding year. Is that something new?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. It has been the law. The only amendment is to extend it to fishermen as well as to farmers. The general treatment is the same. In contradistinction to most taxpayers, farmers do not have to make quarterly payments. They can wait until the year is over before paying the estimated amount of the tax, and the final payment is due on April 30 following.
Has consideration been given to deducting from the farmer's income tax the amount he does not get for his produce, to which he is entitled?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think that is a matter which has been given consideration recently.
It is about time it was considered.

Many of us come in daily contact with farmers, and one of the difficulties is that those who are making the laws governing farmers do not know enough about agriculture to make those laws really applicable to people living on the land. The farmers throughout the dominion are always ready to obey the law. There are no more law-abiding people in the country. They want to do the right thing. At the same time, they have a perfect right to ask that they shall not be put into unnecessary straight-jackets by people who may not know anything about agriculture. That is the attitude which most farmers take toward many government regulations.
The^ government has gone into business extensively, in agriculture and other things, and it becomes more important than ever that the officials of the department, or 
those who are making these laws, should receive practical suggestions from bona fide farmers themselves. It is about time that the farmers themselves rvere allowed to make some suggestions as to how matters can best be worked out so far as their own business is concerned. It is not enough to go to a farmer who is a big operator. It is not always best to take advice entirely from someone who is not in the lower brackets of agriculture. The great bulk of the farming community is composed of people who are operating in small units. The department should seek advice of some of the smaller unit farmers in Canada, in order to see how this thing can best be worked out- to the advantage of all.
These farmers come to members from time to time with many suggestions. The government departments are too far removed from the ordinary dirt farmers with regard to income tax forms and income tax levies. When a farmer, who has hardly enough time to do his ordinary work, is asked to go into big business almost and have his income tax return filled out in the same way as they are filled out by people who have bookkeepers, accountants and all that sort of thing, it is something that does not- work with him. He needs something far simpler than that, or else he may have to go out of business. He cannot afford to carry a huge bookkeeping organization on the farm. He has enough trouble now to make ends meet without being faced with that necessity.
There must be a way out of this. I do not wish to be unnecessarily critical, but I should like to see if this government and parliament cannot get down to some kind of basis whereby the farmer will be able to find out what he is required to pay without going through all this terrible period of misery, one could almost call it, that those engaged in agriculture all over Canada must go through before they put in their income tax returns. I shall make a suggestion to the minister. This government spends a great deal of money on other things which are not nearly as important as this is.
I think it would be a good thing for the minister to cut out some of this red tape and to bring here, at the expense of the government, a few dozen good small-unit farmers and get their advice with regard to what they think should be done in this matter. Having done that, the government should follow their advice, instead of that of some of these high-ranking officials who perhaps never saw a farm.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friend brought this matter up, because the Department of Finance is not nearly as devoid as some may think of officials who have some interest and background in practical farming.

Income Tax Act
The assistant deputy minister of finance who sits in front of me here today, and who is in charge of taxation, was born and brought up on a farm. His brother still runs it; and it was his father's farm. The assistant deputy minister of justice, who sits in front of me today, was born and brought up in a little village in Saskatchewan. The brother of the deputy minister of finance still runs the family farm in Glengarry county, not far from here. Even the Minister of Finance himself was brought up in a small town, and lived' on a farm from the time he was five years of age until he was thirteen. He learned to milk a cow; and, while it is true that he has not been in constant contact with the farming community, I can assure members of the committee that he knows something about the problems of the small farmer.
There was no income tax then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I just mention that to show that the department is not staffed by people who have not had some practical experience on the farm.
May I follow that point up with the minister? I am terribly serious about this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: So am I.

I am not making a light suggestion to the minister, because every person representing an agricultural section of Canada is faced with this important problem. It is also important from the general point of view of our citizenry at large that the income tax form be reduced to some simple terms so that there will be satisfaction as between agriculture and the government which is collecting the taxes. While the minister and all his deputies may have been brought up on farms, so was I; and when I go back to the farm now, I find that there have been a great many improvements and a great many changes in agriculture. More than that, as somebody pointed out a little while ago, in those days-in my day and in the minister's-we had to master a great many other practical things on the farm, but we certainly did not have to spend as much time as the average farmer now must in making out the infernal income tax forms that only a Philadelphia lawyer could possibly understand. I ask the minister why he does not accept my suggestion, bring some dirt farmers here and get their views.
How about a few fishermen?

The expenditure for that purpose, I would say, would be the best bit
of expenditure the government has made. It is important that the good will of agriculture be obtained with respect to the income tax just the same as it is important that the good will of other sections of the population should be obtained. Do not be unreasonable about the matter. The farmers want^ to do the fair thing, but they want to do it in a way which is practical for them and for the government as well. I make that serious suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I know my hon. friend is serious. He will recall that two or three v ears ago when the question of farmers' income tax returns first became a serious matter, the^ tax branch consulted the Department of Agriculture, called the farm organizations in, and discussed the matter at length. The net result was that a six-page form was produced, instead of a four-page one.
You did not have one of the people I am now suggesting.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not suggesting this in a joking way. It is in the interests, not only of the farmers but of all the taxpayers, to have the forms as simple as possible. At the same time, the reasons that any income tax form is complex is in order to make the tax equitable. The simplest thing in the world is to make a flat percentage tax and say to the people that they will pay that tax, with no deductions for anything. But when you include deductions for depreciation, for medical expenses, for this and for that, then of necessity you get into a complicated form. That is what creates the difficulty. I am in complete agreement with my hon. friend that, whether it relates to the farmer, to the wage earner or anybody else, efforts should be made to have the forms just as simple as they can possibly be made.

I cannot believe that the officials who were responsible for drafting section 45 (a) can have had any experience whatsoever in grain farming. That section gives two alternatives, and they are both bad. Let me read the section:
(a) on or before December 31 in each taxation year, two-thirds of the tax as estimated by him at the rates for the year on his estimated taxable income for the year or on his taxable income for the immediately preceding year.
Let us take the first one of those. He should estimate what his income will be and pay two-thirds by December 31. I think the minister more than anybody else will appreciate the difficulty farmers are having today in filling out their income tax forms. They
Income Tax Act

are having plenty of difficulty in filling them out by April 30. Before a farmer can possibly estimate what his income will be, he will have to fill out that form. Therefore you are asking him to fill out that form-he does not have to mail it, but he must fill it out in order to find out what his income will be- in order that he may pay two-thirds of it by the end of December. I suggest that will be a difficult thing, because he will find it hard enough to have these forms completed by April 30. Then the section gives the following alternative:
... or on his taxable income for the immediately preceding year . . .
That is, of course, absolute and utter nonsense. How can anybody suggest that the income of a farmer last year is a guide to what his income may be this year? If he is a grain farmer, for instance, last year he may have threshed forty bushels to the acre, which would give him a good income. This year he may be hailed out. and have no income at all. How could the department possibly suggest that a return for last year will be any guide whatever as to his income this year? The returns vary from year to year. They vary from five per cent-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That same thing applies with regard to other occupations. In other occupations an estimate has to be made at the end of the first quarter.

Yes. But the minister will admit that the farming industry is a difficult one. Especially is that true with regard to .grain farming, because practically the whole return conies in, in the fall of the year. I will frankly admit that I have never sent in two-thirds at the end of the year. I did not even know that I was supposed to do that; and I doubt if one per cent of the farmers today realize that they are supposed to send in two-thirds of the amount of their tax at the end of the year. I have never been notified. I have regularly sent in my income tax in April.
I have never received a letter from the taxation blanch telling me I should have sent in t\\o-thirds of the tax by the end of December. Why? Nor have I been charged interest, or at least I have never been notified that interest was being charged. Is it actually the law today that the farmer should sent in two-thirds of his tax by the end of December? If so, how many farmers are doing so? What is the penalty for not doing so? And if there is no penalty, why should the farmer do it? Ceitainly I think that point needs clarification.
I do not know of a single farmer who sends m two-thirds of his tax by the end of 
December. They wait until April, and they do not feel very happy about sending it in even then.
So I suggest that the minister could very well wipe out that provision as far as farmers are concerned. I do not believe more than a very small fraction of the farmers are complying with it, and I think the minister will agree that they are finding it hard enough to have their income taxes paid by April. Why put in a clause which can do nothing more than irritate the farmers? You are just going out of your way to put in a little section to get them mad, just as you did when you put out that net worth statement. You got them so mad that you finally had to withdraw it. Do not wait until they get mad about this. The only reason they are not mad about it is that they do not know it is there. If you start trying to force the farmers to send in two-thirds of their tax by the end of December you will meet with just about the same kind of reception as you got when you sent out that net worth statement. So I suggest that it would be far better to withdraw this section and tell the farmers to have their income tax returns in by the end of April.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This section has been in the act since 1943, I do not want to irritate the farmers any more than anyone else, but I do not think the farmer is entitled to any extraordinary or special treatment.
But he gets it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He gets it in many cases. The average taxpayer has to pay his tax by instalments. At the beginning of the year he has to estimate what his income will be, and he has to pay one-quarter of the tax at the end of the first three months, another quarter at the end of six months, another quarter at the end of nine months, and the balance by December 31. The farmer gets special consideration here. He does not have to pay any of his tax until the end of the calendar year, and then he has an option. He can estimate his tax on his estimated income and pay three-quarters of it, or he can take his last year's income and pay the tax on three-quarters of that, paying the balance by April oO. I think that is fair. We are deducting from the salary and wage earner day after day, month after month as he goes along. We require instalment payments by those who receive income from interest and dividends. We make lawyers and other professional men who are on a fee basis pay in quarterly instalments, and I think this is fair for the farmer.
I do not believe the farmers of this country want special privileges.

Income Tax Act
They want some sense shown in these matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think I am right in that; I believe I am.

There is all the difference in the world. You talk about someone in a secondary industry paying on a quarterly basis. The grain farmer does not get any return until the fall. If he had to make a quarterly return he would show certain expenses without any returns, and at the end of the half year he would show the same thing. His returns do not come in until the fall of the year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know much about grain farming, but how many farmers in western Canada or elsewhere have not sold their crop by December 31?
There would be very few farmers who had not sold their wheat by December 31.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And that is the first time the farmer has to make any payment.
But why ask him to make any payment then? Why not let it go until April?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because other people have started making their payments at the first of the year.
Let the minister answer this question, then. How many farmers are sending in two-thirds of their income tax by the end of the year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not say; that is not my department. I can say that the law is, and has been for five years, that the farmer should send in two-thirds of his tax at the end of the calendar year.
And they are not doing it, because they do not know the provision is there. Apparently the income tax branch have not notified them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Other income taxpayers
know what the law is. I do not know why the farmer should not know about it. Special booklets are sent out explaining the law, and I believe the farmers are learning quickly.
Does the booklet in connection with farm income tell them they must pay two-thirds of their tax by the end of the year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course it does.

But my point is that the farmers do not know about it. Perhaps they
should, but they do not, and they are not sending in that percentage. The thing I cannot understand is why the income tax branch have not notified the farmers, when they receive their tax returns in April, that they should have sent in a certain percentage of the tax by the end of December. They are not doing so. I have never paid anything in December, and I did not know I had to. Nor have I ever received any notice from the income tax branch.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The only explanation I can give is that, of course, there has been a tremendous increase in the number of returns. Until the assessors get at the returns and see what has been the record of payment, they do not appreciate or realize that an instalment payment has not been made. I think that situation will correct itself pretty soon, as the taxpayers realize their obligations. The only point I am making is that, if anything, this is a rule which works in favour of the farmer and fisherman as against other types of enterprise.
I do not think it does, because they are not comparable.

I want to support wholeheartedly what has been said by the previous speaker. If the minister had been on a farm in the last few years when income tax forms had to be made out; if he had to keep the books which are necessary in order to make out those forms, I think he would be more willing to listen to our complaints in this regard. I have made out income tax forms for several years, and I never knew we were supposed to send in two-thirds of our tax by the end of December. I, in common with the last speaker, never received any notice. The farmer is the greatest gambler in this country. At the first of the year, when he plants his seed, he never knows whether he will get a crop, nor does he know what he will be paid for it. To ask him to make a payment in six months-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Twelve months; he can wait until the end of the year.
And in many cases at the end of the year he has not sold the crop.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then it goes into the next year, anyway, if he is on a cash basis. I do not know whether members of the committee appreciate it, but this is a part of the pay-as-you-go tax plan put into operation in 1943, when those earning salaries and wages were compelled to have a portion of those salaries and wages taken out each week or month,
Income Tax Act

depending upon the pay period, as a tax payment. In the case of investors and businessmen, payment was to be on a quarterly basis. In the case of farmers and fishermen, they pay two-thirds at the end of the year, and then they have another three months in which to pay the balance. I do not know; perhaps my ideas of what is fair are all wrong, but it seems to me that is eminently fair and reasonable. Certainly if you contrast the farmer with the wage earner, the worker in the city, it is more than fair. The farmers may not know about it, but I cannot see that it is unfair.
Mr. QUEtLOH: But the wage earner gets his wage every week or every month. The grain farmer gets his returns at the end of the year, and he does not get any money until then. To say he should pay money each month would be utter nonsense.

I should like to support the remarks of the previous speakers with respect to this clause. I can assure the minister I have had a number of letters from farmer constituents of mine; and while no one likes to pay taxes, these letters express far greater objection to the nature of the form they have to fill out than to the tax itself. It is perfectly true that it has created a great- deal of ill-feeling. We want to avoid ill-feeling where we can; but I can assure the minister that this feeling is widespread among farmers in the west, including those in my own riding. As I say, I have had many letters dealing with this matter.

As other hon. members have said, I believe farmers who are eligible for taxation are prepared to pay it. But they are hesitant because, if they make returns, some smart mathematician who does not know anything about farming may trip them up. A farmer, who may have made out his return with the very best of intentions, will find himself in difficulty.
Another thing which bothers him is that it may be four or five years before he obtains a clearance for his return. No business, except the taxation branch, can be carried on in that way. I can see no reason in the world why returns should not be cleared in the calendar year in which they are filed; not four or five years later, at a time when a man cannot remember where he stood.
This government has socialism beat a mile. It is a partner in every enterprise that wins, but it is not a partner in the enterprise that loses. If a socialist government were to take office it would have to participate in the losses as well as in the gains. Farmers complain that in the years when they have good

crops they are penalized, and they wonder why they should continue to produce. I think this form should be simplified.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Hon. members will appreciate that most of the discussion would be more appropriate on the estimates of the Minister of National Revenue, because this matter concerns him primarily. It is not the concern of the Minister of Finance. While I do not wish to curtail discussion, it is not my personal responsibility to look after those matters, and I should think that hon. members might discuss them under the estimates of the Department of National Revenue.
This makes it necessary for the farmer to make out his income tax before December 30?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It does not.

To estimate two-thirds of his tax, he could not possibly do so without doing that. In effect it is asking him to make out two sets of forms in the same year [DOT]-and one is bad enough. I would add, further, that I subscribe to wThat was said earlier with respect to having a farm background for inspectors. I would urge that any inspectors going out to farmers-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member knows, of course, that this does not come within my department.
I realize that; but it has been mentioned before and I should like to have my views on record. Inspectors going out to interview farmers should, by all means, have a farm background.

While it is not the responsibility of the Minister of Finance to collect the tax, it is the responsibility of the minister and' his department to see that taxes are assessed on a realistic basis. What has been said emphasizes the fact that income tax laws are not realistic when applied to farming. I would refer the minister to what happened in 1942 and 1943. In those years the government regulations prohibited farmers from delivering their grain. They were put on a quota basis, and were allowed to deliver five bushels per authorized acre. The remainder of the grain was held on the farms. In those years the farmer suffered a loss on the operation of his business, so far as cash income was concerned. Then in 1944 he was told to deliver all he could. The quota was opened up, and immediately the farmer was placed in the income tax brackets, through the income he had received in that one year.
I believe one would find a good 'deal of protest throughout the countiy, because the laws applying to farm incomes do not consider

Income Tax Act
the peculiar nature of the occupation of farming as a business, as differentiated from other types of business, or even from the man who earns his income as an employee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are allowed the five-year average.

Yes. I know the average is allowed. I think it will be found that at the present time many farmers are asking that the law be altered, so that they may make some kind of payment on their income tax when they deliver grain or other produce. It might be arranged so that, when the extent of their exemption is reached, a certain proportion might be taken from the receipts from their deliveries over and above that amount.
We can deal with the collection of income tax when we are discussing the estimates of the Department of National Revenue, but I do protest that the legislation respecting farm incomes is entirely out of line with the whole business of farming; and the farming community resents very much the present set-up.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 46-Other individuals.

I should like to make a protest with regard to this section. Under the section it appears that every individual, with the exception of those to whom section 44 (2) and section 45 apply, must pay their income tax in four equal quarterly instalments on March 31, June 30, September 30 and December 31. If one does not pay the tax of those dates, interest is charged for the remainder of the year.
During the war the practice of requiring quarterly payments of income tax grew up. As I remember it, the arrangement was a voluntary one. It was with some considerable shock, therefore, that I learned the other day in committee that now the quarterly payment of the tax is compulsory, as is shown on the form which was shown to me by the Minister of National Revenue.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat was right when he said that the collection of the tax must be realistic. Speaking personally, I find it difficult to estimate the tax each quarter as I go along. I, for one, would like to be in a position to look at a little bit of money as I accumulate it before I have to pay it out. I believe the people of the country generally do not know that if they do not pay their tax payments at these quarterly instalment periods they must pay interest on that money at a rate of five or six per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has been four per cent in the past.
The people should understand and should be told.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is four per cent until January 1, 1949.
I do not think this a realistic procedure. People in this country are having a real struggle to pay income tax and to pay it almost before they get the money in their hands.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That happens to every salary and wage earner.

The salary and wage
earners know what they are getting from day to day. Other people, including small merchants, people in business and those in the professions have a hard time to find out exactly what they get every three months. It seems to me that this is too harsh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am familiar with tire problem. When I wras paying income tax from the practice of law I had the same difficulty the hon. member has described in estimating what my income would be over the year. Nevertheless I made my quarterly payments.

Mr. Chairman, from the way the minister has expressed himself I would suggest, with all deference, that the minister is probably a little too optimistic in his views about farmers. I was raised on a farm and have experienced the ups and downs of farming. I know there is a tremendous amount of uncertainty in all matters relating to farming, and in that respect the farmer is in an entirely different position. Consequently, in the matter of paying taxes he should be given the utmost consideration.
There are farmers with good land who have found just the right way to farm it and who, therefore get a good income every year, but other farmers three or four miles away who do not happen to have the same kind of land or perhaps do not work it the right way, or through no fault of their own, through hail or frost and other vicissitudes, get little or no income at all.
Take the area I live in. The farmers in some parts could not get on their land this year until after the 1st of June. Naturally they are in great uncertainty. No one can tell what thej' will be able to make. That is just one illustration. There is drought, disease, wind, insects and all that kind of thing entering into a farmer's life besides adverse prices and markets. Do not let the idea get abroad that farmers ought to be treated on the same basis as other producers in the country. The farmer's lot is, at the
Income Tax Act

very best, a very hard and precarious one; that goes for the vast percentage, from seventy-five to eighty per cent, of the farmers throughout this land, and it is usually that seventy-five to eighty per cent who are the ones who are worried almost to death in making out income tax forms and struggling to clear themselves from a lot of official interference. It is these people about whom I am greatly concerned, not the few fortunate ones who are able to get along.
I say once more, let us be as considerate of our farmers as we possibly can be. A discussion took place in the house the other day as to why we had fallen down in butter production. One of the main reasons is the income tax structure. The farmer milks his cows at night after a long day's work, and again in the morning before a long day's work, and all of it is done in his overtime. To take the income which that man happens to make, perhaps a few hundred dollars, from the milking he does, and to add that to his income and increase his income tax accordingly, is just pure mismanagement of the nation's affairs. If we cannot talk that fact into the government, it will be knocked into the government by a deficiency in production, and by that time it will be too late, because the means will be out of the farmers' hands to produce such commodities as milk, butter, eggs, beef and pork. It is my settled opinion, after talking with a great number of farmers in my constituency and in other parts, that this uncertainty about production which is worrying us so much today is largely the result of the income tax regulations.

I wish to thank the minister for the background that he has been good enough to give us today with respect to his officials. However, a lot of the trouble we are running into over the income tax forms is not the result of the officials in front of him but is due to a man named Brown, from Winnipeg, who was a former banker.
The income tax is complicated to the last degree, but the hon. member for Lethbridge has given a very good illustration of how it works out in practice. If the minister would go around my constituency with me and talk to the farmers he would find not dozens but hundreds of them who would tell him that the situation pointed out by the hon. member for Lethbridge is a true picture of the actual conditions.
The-farmer is in a class by himself. He is not looking for special privileges. He keeps a few cows as a sideline and has to be up milking them at six o'clock in the morning before he goes out into the fields, and then

milk them again at night after his day's work in the field. On many farms the children help with the milking. If something is not done to relieve the income tax burden on the farmers, production wall be curtailed a lot more yet. We must be realistic and try to find the cause for decreased farm production. It is largely because of the income tax. Provision must be made to encourage production by giving the farmer and his children the same opportunity that other people have. The man who lives in a city and has five or six boys under sixteen very often has one of his boys peddling papers; another will be running errands for some store, and all of them have an opportunity of making a good many dollars on the side, which is never counted as part of the family income. But the farmer and his family are considered as one unit, and the father pays the penalty in increased taxation. Some change must be made in the income tax if the farmers are to be encouraged to produce more farm products.

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman. As president of an insurance company, I know this will be a hardship on the smaller companies. We do not know what our risk will be. Sometimes it may be 86.000; sometimes it may be $20,000. In my own company we have $5,000,000 of risk. We are running on twenty cents a hundred, and have our surplus of $40,000 in values. Suppose we make two cents a hundred, $2 on $100. On the $10,000 of our surplus every year we have that income. We may have a loss of $6,000. Say we have a surplus of $2,000. The minister himself raised the question of co-operatives, but is he not in this legislation assisting them to build up reserves, by means which I need not mention in detail, and is that not substantially what this mutual company is asking for? I would hope, notwithstanding the fact that the minister says he has considered it, that he might consider it again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The provisions of this act extend to mutual insurance companies. Section 67 extends to mutual insurance companies and to any corporation. Section 67 may indirectly help mutual insurance companies along with other mutual corporations, but there is no change at all, and the essence of what is desired is to create reserves out of tax-free income. If that can be done under section 67, well and good. I do not know that it can, but that is the only section under which it can be done. As a general rule, that is not the principle followed in the taxation law.

If the taxpayer finds that he must employ outside help in order to keep his books, is he allowed to deduct the money he pays for that purpose as an expense from his income? The reason I ask the question is this. While technically the money is not spent in earning the income, the man would not be free to devote himself to earning income, likely at a much higher rate, if he had to keep track of his own accounts so that he would be able to fill out his income tax return at the proper time. I should like the minister to answer whether or not he is allowed to deduct those expenses as a legitimate item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would depend. If he is in 'business, he is entitled to deduct his bookkeeping expenses, the same as any other expenses. If he was purely an investor; if he simply holds stocks and bonds, I do not think he is entitled to the cost of keeping a record of his investment receipts.

It seems absurd that he is not allowed to do so, because if he has to keep a double-entry system himself, as he must if he is to keep accurate books, he will have to devote much of his time to that type of work; whereas he is much better employed, from the standpoint of the treasury as well as himself, if he sticks to his own knitting and lets somebody else do that piece of work which is perhaps not directly attributable, as I pointed out in my explanation, to bringing in the income.
I hope the minister will give consideration to that point, because, a great many people find they cannot look after their own books.
They do not know how to do double-entry bookkeeping, to begin with, so that if they are to know where they stand, particularly in relation to the revenue department, they must employ outsiders to keep their books for them. Surely that is a legitimate expense which they should be allowed. Otherwise a man must take his own time to do the work and cannot earn as much; so he would not be in as high a bracket for the purposes of the income tax branch as would be the case otherwise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Does the minister not think a ten-day limit is rather short? It is all right in districts where a person is close to the post office, or where there are good roads. As the minister is aware, however, there are many areas, especially in western Canada, where at times it is almost impossible to traverse the roads to reach the post office. Your neighbour may bring out your regular mail in the ordinary course, but he would not be able to bring out a registered letter, which would have to wait until you went for it. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
An amendment was made to this clause in committee, and I promised to give consideration to a further amendment before the bill was considered by the committee of the whole. The amendment made by the banking and commerce committee inserted the word "main" in the second line of the section, so that it will read:
Where the treasury board has decided that one of the main purposes for a transaction or transactions effected before the coming into force of this act was avoidance or reduction of taxes . . .
In committee I suggested that I might be prepared further to amend this section by

Income Tax Act
putting the word "improper" before "avoidance or reduction", so that it would read, "was improper avoidance or reduction of taxes". 1 am prepared to ask one of my colleagues to move such an amendment. In order to give effect to the amendment, however, I would add a further subsection as subsection 6, which would read:
An avoidance or reduction of tax may be regarded as improper for the purposes of this section although it is not illegal.
The reason for the amendment is that the word "improper" might be interpreted as meaning "illegal". The evil which this section seeks to correct is that by legal but rather devious means an avoidance or reduction of tax may be accomplished which should not be accomplished. In its present form the section has been in the act since, I think, 1943. It came in, in wartime. It was in the act in another form before that, and in its present form it came in, in 1943. I am prepared, according to the undertaking I gave, to ask one of my colleagues to move this further amendment.

I am going to say just a few words about this section, because it seems to. me that it goes much farther than even the rapacity of the tax gatherer can justify. The language is simple, it makes a crime of seeking a reduction in one's income tax. We discussed this matter at some length in the banking and commerce committee. I assume that the law will be fairly interpreted and that it will be appliedi, as we believe all our laws are, with justice and with the utmost care. But why it should be suggested that a person who seeks, under the law, a reduction in his income tax is a person concerning whom a direction may be made, is a little difficult to understand.
The wording of 126 (1) is:
Where the treasury board has decided that one of the-
And the minister has suggested an amendment.
*-purposes for a transaction or transactions effected before or after the coming into force of this act was avoidance or reduction of taxes

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The word "improper" was added.

Yes.

improper avoidance or reduction of taxes that might otherwise have become payable under this act . . .
And so on. He suggests that the word "improper" be defined; and "improper", as I understand the amendment, is not to be interpreted as "illegal". The transaction may be 5849-364J
legal and still be improper. I suggest that this is not only putting the court in a difficult situation but admitting the inability of parliament to enact effective legislation. It places in the hands of treasury board the power to write a direction whenever it wishes; because the only condition of such a direction is that the taxpayer shall seek a reduction in taxes which treasury board may call improper, but which is not illegal.
I regret very much to see legislation go on the statute books which gives to officialdom the right to penalize where there is no illegality; and that is the position which the committee is now being asked to assume. It is more or less fashionable these days to abuse officials and refer to them as bureaucrats. Be that as it may, this section is an evidence of a desire to have one's way, despite the law. It is a statement by parliament that officialdom shall reign, whatever the law says. That, Mr. Chairman, is a further encroachment upon fundamental liberties and civil rights which the House of Commons should resent.
We have gone through a number of sections hastily this afternoon, more hastily than wisdom would dictate. But when we are blandly asked to enact legislation which, regardless of its meaning, says, "Somebody is going to have the right to penalize you and to issue a document which, when it goes before the tribunal which revises these matters, may not be revised"-because the appeal board has no right to revise a direction-then I say we are going too far.
I move, therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Kamloops:
That section 126 in the bill be deleted and that section 32A in the old act be substituted therefor.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are repeating what took place in the committee on banking and commerce. I must congratulate the hon. member for Stanstead. He is in his best oratorical form this afternoon and has just made a most impressive presentation of the evils of this section.
It deserves it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Those of us who were in the house in 1943, however, will recall equally clearly the speech made by the then minister of finance, in which he pointed out the evils of tax evasion, and the advantage which was being taken of loopholes in the law which it had been impossible to foresee, and which necessitated the introduction of this section.
I shall not attempt to repeat the arguments put forward at that time or those which I offered the other day in the committee on banking and commerce. But I wish to say
Income Tax Act

this, that the resourcefulness of those who wish to avoid or to reduce their taxation liability is practically unlimited. One tries as best one can to keep plugging up the loopholes in the income tax legislation; but it is not quite possible to keep up with the resourcefulness of individuals such as I have described.
I have agreed to the insertion of the word "improper", which is the only change from the existing section 32A. In effect the section as it now appears in the bill-
Plus the limitation of the word "improper".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend wishes me to withdraw my amendment I shall withdraw it. The section would then be in exactly the same terms as section 32A. The amendment has been proposed because I wish to meet the views held by members of the committee that the section does authorize broad powers. But the purpose the section is intended to achieve is an important one. In these days when we are taxing the wages and salaries of people with small incomes I think we should have every necessary weapon to prevent avoidance or the reduction of taxation by the more well-to-do taxpayers. That is the reason for this section.
I am quite prepared to have my colleague propose the amendment I have suggested; but if the committee does not want that, we shall go back to the wording of section 32A.

I ask you to call it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are dealing with clause 126.

Mr. Chairman, when the house rose at six o'clock I was about to discuss this section a little more in detail. My hon. friend, the Minister of Finance, has found that I have injected a little enthusiasm into my utterances. I can tell him that there are some things which do arouse me. When I see what seems to me to be a challenge to law and to order and to the very basis of our system of government, the British system, a system evolved by the British, a system which we helped to develop; when I see what I consider not only a challenge but a violation of the supremacy of law, I do become disturbed.
My hon. friend has suggested an amendment to the income tax bill which will subject the taxpayer to the direst penalties, although he

may not have broken the law. To achieve that purpose, the minister has worded the law in such a way that any person who seeks a reduction in the tax-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: An improper reduction.

My hon. friend says, "an improper reduction". Let it be said that he has inserted a clause defining "improper" in a way that makes it clear that "improper" does not mean "illegal". "Impropriety" as used in the amendment does not mean "illegality", whatever else it may mean. The result is that we have a law which, 'although not broken, may subject a person who has acted within it to a fine and to the payment of taxes that are not exigible under the law.
That is a matter which arouses a great deal of trepidation in anyone who is attached to and appreciates the real significance of what we have been pleased to call the rule of law. This section is a direct attack upon the rule of law; it is a violation of it. It says that if an individual, in the view of the treasury board, has sought a reduction of 'taxes-
And hon. MEMBER: An avoidance.

No, not avoidance only; a person who seeks avoidance or a person who does not seek avoidance but who seeks a reduction improperly is liable to the sanctions of the section. But "improperly" does not mean "illegally". So it means that a person who seeks a reduction legally may be prosecuted.
This means that we are reverting to the Star Chamber method. It means that the taxpayer of this country who happens to be out of favour with the authorities who man the treasury board may be made a criminal without breaking the law, may be punished and fined a large amount although not without the law. I say to this committee that this is a most serious departure from everything that we have believed existed in this country, of everything about which we have boasted in this country.
We all sit here very quietly. Most of us are anxious to get away. We have been here since last December. We are weary; we are anxious; we are overburdened; but here we are, most of us unaware of the, I was going to say, irretrievable step that we are taking. Most of us appear to be completely apathetic. Do we realize that we are putting back into the hands of an element entirely beyond the control of parliament, rights, privileges and prerogatives which were wrested from uncontrolled authority centuries ago?
Liberty is something that cannot be toyed with. We have not had it very long in this

Income Tax Act
country, and we have seen it seriously violated in the last few years, so much so that a great deal of the time of this house, the time of this committee and the time of the united nations has been spent in discussing human rights and elemental freedoms. Yet, without apparent interest and with complete apathy, this house is writing into our taxing law an iniquitous invasion of private rights and of human freedoms.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This section has been in the law since 1943, and the proposed amendment I would think makes the section less objectionable from my hon. friend's point of view.
Mr. HACIvETT: My hon. friend was very patient with me. I wish he would not say that this section has been in the law since 1943, because that is a complete inaccuracy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All right. The section which is proposed in this bill is somewhat less objectionable. I would think, from my hon. friend's point of view than the section which has been in the law since 1943. The section which has been in the law since 1943, section 32A, provides:
Where the treasury board is of the opinion that the main purpose for which any transaction or transactions was or were effected . . . was the avoidance or reduction of liability to tax, it may, if it thinks fit, direct that such adjustment . . .
The proposed section in the bill is:
Where the treasury board has decided that one of the main purposes for a transaction or transactions effected before or after the coming into force of this act was . . .
And I am suggesting "improper avoidance of a tax." That has been in the law since 1943 in a form which I think is somewhat more rigorous than the form I am suggesting here. It was put into the law because of a fact which we discovered. There were these elaborate schemes for tax avoidance which were difficult, if not impossible, to spell out in the law itself. I think there har e been only three or four cases in which this section has been availed of, but I remember one case very well where, by a combination of three or four companies set up in Nassau and Panama, and one or two other places, a Canadian resident was able to avoid legally the payment of some $2 million tax. This section was availed of to bring that taxpayer before the treasury board to show cause why he should not pay these taxes. It was not taken any further; the taxes were paid. It was legal; but on any basis of justice, fairness, or whatever adjective one wants to use, that Canadian resident should not have been able to avoid payment of that $2 million of taxes.
I have asserted this before; I assert it again, and my predecessor has done the same thing, that no person, by using the loopholes which the law may offer, should be able to avoid the payment of his just share of the responsibilities for carrying the burden and the costs of carrying on the business of the country.
One may say, if it is legal, if it complies with the formal requirements of the law, then he should be able to do so. Well, perhaps so; but in the light of experience, it was found that a section of this kind was essential if practices of the kind which I have indicated were to be prevented.
There is an appeal from the findings of the treasury board in this matter to the Exchequer Court of Canada. The exchequer court can hear any evidence it sees fit to hear, can review the findings of treasury board and can come to the conclusion that one of the main purposes of the transactions involved was not the avoidance or reduction of taxation. So far as I am personally concerned, I think it is a section which should stay in the law, and I am proposing it for that reason.
As I have said, a corresponding section, one perhaps somewhat less rigorous from the lawyer's point, of view, has been in the law for five years. I will ask one of my colleagues to move the amendment which I have suggested, and I say, Mr. Chairman, that is as far as I am prepared to go in connection with the section.

I should like to add a word or two on this subject. The minister has made a clever
speech-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: An honest speech.

-putting forward a view of this principle which it is awfully easy to accept. I believe that I dislike as much as anybody people who resort to clever devices within the law to escape income tax. I believe that we should have the best and ablest people in the service of the government to defeat these things. On the other hand, to say that, it seems to me, is a whole world different from saying you are going to give to certain people a power above the law. That seems to me to lead us into a situation to which there is no end. I said the other night in committee, and I repeat, that if we could be sure that we would have a man like the Minister of Finance always administering a law such as this I would have very little fear of it. But many people in Canada know, as I know, that there has been, in this country a government inspired by vindictiveness almost beyond belief in taxing,

Income Tax Act
so that decent people went in fear of, one [DOT]might say their lives, because an extreme law was used in a vindictive way.
There is no exaggeration in what the hon. member for Stanstead has said, that once people are given power above the law, one does not know where it stops. The case which the minister gave, of course one hates; but we are setting one case of that kind against the unlimited number of other cases which might be affected in the circumstances in which it has been set up.
Let us look at another thing. The minister says that this was set up in 1943. He says it has been used four times since then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Do not hold me to the number. I know of four cases.

That is what the official said the other night. I remember that, beca'use I was so struck with it that this had happened so seldom. Incidentally,. I think that is a great tribute to the honesty of the taxpayer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Or the effectiveness of the section.

Let us go back to what we are actually doing. It has been said much better than I can say it by a learned judge administering the law that you cannot begin to say what is the spirit of the law. You are either within the law, or you are without the law. Once you leave that, it seems to me that you are exactly out on the uncharted sea which the hon..member for Stanstead has told us about.
Before I take my seat I want to say just one thing. To me, as to the hon. member for Stanstead, it is disturbing to a degree, first of all to find the. minister, for whom we all have great respect, taking this so lightly; to have other people in the house whose hearts I respect though not always their heads, taking the view that, just because you will occasionally have a sharp and, to my mind, am unworthy kind of man, who tries to sail close to the wind, and who will get an advantage in spite of all the able officials that we shall have, get an advantage which will be very shortlived because the law will be very quick in overtaking him, for that reason we are to maintain this section which was put in as a war measure; and we are to go on doing this in the name of fairness. We are to do this tiling which takes us back to the powers the hon. member has referred to, and which I think were summarized in the old days by saying that the law depended on the length of the chancellor's foot. In other words, the law was not known; it was made by the feel-

ings of the man who administered it. When you have good men doing that it is bad enough; 'but when you have bad men doing it, as you may have one day, then there is no limit to the evil.

As the hon. member who has the honour of seconding the amendment moved by the hon. member for Stanstead, I wish to say a few words on this section. First, it seems to me, from what the minister has said just now and before the dinner recess, that his position with respect to this section, and to the amendment which he has moved, is based on the principle that legislation should be drafted on the basis that there are a few fraudulent people in the country who will take advantage of every loophole. That is a proposition of fact, the belief in the existence of those few fraudulent people, which may or may not be true. But my first quarrel with the principle and with the practical application of this section is that that is a false proposition on which to base legislation, because I think our law should not be made for people such as that. Our law must be made to benefit the honest majority.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This section does not affect the honest majority.

This section does affect the honest majority in spite of what the minister says, because it is applied to the honest majority just as much as it is applied to the fraudulent few, if there be those fraudulent few who seek to take advantage of the law. That is an inherent weakness in much of the law we find in the country today, and I believe, as strongly as I can believe anything, that our income tax law especially, which applies to every person in the land, must be so designed as to meet the case of the average taxpayer who dislikes paying taxes. That is a healthy sign, for it would be unfortunate for the country if we reached the point where people liked paying taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a long way off.

Our law must be designed *to meet the case of the average taxpayer, who is not fraudulent, and must not be so designed, on a general basis, that in order to catch the occasional few we put ourselves in the position of doing injustice to the honest majority. But that is the position in which this section puts us because, as the hon. member for Stanstead pointed out, it places the treasury board and the enforcing officials beyond the ordinary law. It puts them in the position of making the law, and it is not this House of Commons that makes the law.

Income Tax Act
The house makes the law and the treasury board says, it does not matter what the law is; it does not matter whether you have followed the law, whether you have done even those things which the minister himself, in the banking and commerce committee, said were perfectly legal; because you have done them, we say you have done them for an improper purpose and we hold you liable.
Because I believe that is a false principle on which to proceed; because I am of the opinion that if there be loopholes that can be taken advantage of i't is better to go on plugging the loophole until eventually we arrive at something that is as near perfection as we can achieve, instead of leaving the loopholes wide open and leaving it 'to the discretion of -the treasury board to plug those loopholes as it sees fit-because I so believe, I have pleasure in seconding the amendment and shall vote for it when it is put to the vote.

I cannot agree with what has been said by the hon. member for Stan-stead and the hon. member for Kamloops. In fact I suggest 'to the minister that he drop the amendment and leave the language as it is, because in my opinion "improper avoidance" implies proper avoidance, and I cannot imagine that there could be a proper avoidance brought about by some .taxpayer purposely scheming to avoid taxation. And that is all this section means. I think it is proper and necessary. What about the millions of other taxpayers who make their returns properly and withoW scheming ito avoid or even cause a reduction in their taxation?
They are as much subject to this as anyone else.
I agree with the minister that no honest taxpayer need fear the section. I think we should pass the bill as it is.

amendment, it seems to me that one appeal this evening was made on the ground that this was contrary to some of the principles of British law.
