speechtext:
Section 50.
On section 50-General.

I appreciate very much the generosity of the committee in allowing this clause to stand this afternoon while I had to be in another committee meeting. I shall try to keep my remarks within short compass. The effect of section 50 is to increase the rate of interest for the penalty for late payment of taxes from four to six per cent in one case and from six to seven per cent in the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In committee it was amended to seven per cent. That remains unchanged.
It was six to eight per cent. It was amended in the banking and commerce committee and it is six to seven per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. I agreed to that amendment.

We have this position, then. If a taxpayer completes his assessment, sends it in with a cheque in full for the amount of the tax which he has assessed, some months later the department, having reviewed his assessment, may send him out a notice of the revised assessment and notify him that he has underpaid the tax as the department has assessed

it; and then he is liable to pay interest at six per cent for the period in which the tax has been underpaid.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With a limit of twenty months.

With a limit of twenty months maximum interest penalty. The maximum of twenty months applies to the time the department has been in arrears. If his assessment is not received for more than twenty months-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: After twenty months interest ceases to run.

-interest ceases to run after that time. But the point is that even though it may be the fault of the department, owing to its inability to make the revised assessment in time, the taxpayer still has to pay interest. The interest is raised now to six per cent, whereas before it was four per cent. I should point out that this amendment has not been in the law right along, but is the result of a budget resolution introduced this year and an amendment to the income tax act passed this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was there for years until two years ago.

If the minister will allow me to complete my statement I will cover the point he has in mind. As a result of the budget resolution and the amendment to the income tax act passed this year, the rate was raised from four to six per cent in one case and from six to eight per cent in the other, the eight per cent rate having been reduced to seven per cent in the banking and commerce committee. When this resolution was discussed in the house, the hon. member for St. John-Albert, seconded by myself, introduced an amendment to reduce the interest penalty to the old rate, namely, four and six per cent respectively.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was four per cent and seven per cent. I know my hon. friend wants to be accurate. It was never lower than seven per cent for arrears after notice of assessment.

The amendment to which I refer was ruled out of order at the time it was introduced in the debate on the budget resolution, on the ground that it would upset the balance of ways and means. I propose to move the same amendment at this time, on the following grounds.
First, the extra penalty involved in this increase in the interest rate affects the taxpayer even though he is not himself at fault,

Income Tax Act
even though he has made an honest assessment and paid his assessment in full, and even though the fault is that of the department in its inability-and I use that word advisedly- to get out the revised assessment in time. That is the first ground, that even if the taxpayer is not at fault, he will now pay interest at six per cent as a penalty.
In the second place, I do so on the ground that the minister himself has said, as reported at page 4067 of Hansard, that the interest charge of six per cent is frankly in the nature of a penalty. In other words, there is nothing here designed to increase the amount of taxes collected. The interest rate of six per cent is frankly in the nature of a penalty. Because we think, as we thought at the time when we first introduced the amendment, the taxpayer should not be penalized for the default of the department, I suggest that the interest rate should be reduced to the old rate of four per cent.
With respect to the possibility of this upsetting the balance of ways and means, Mr. Chairman, I think we can confidently say that, in introducing this amendment at this time in this manner, we are not liable to be criticized on that ground, because the bill now before the committee is a codification of income tax procedure. The bill will not become operative until January 1, 1949, and therefore it will not upset the balance of ways and means.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will affect this fiscal year, which does not end until the end of March.
Therefore it cannot possibly affect the balance of ways and means for this year because, may I point out, taxes are collected on the basis of the income of the calendar year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: An instalment is due on March 31.

It is based on the income of people to the end of the calendar year. So this change could not possibly upset the balance of ways and means. In that connection I would point out that, in the minister's own words, it is merely a penalty. He cannot be said, surely, to have predicated his balance of ways and means on the slim chance of collecting a two per cent extra penalty. It is not a tax provision: it is only a penalty provision. So I think the amendment is in order at this time on those grounds, and is well justified on the basis that taxpayers should not be penalized, because the department itself may have occasioned the delay in making the 5849-365
revised assessment. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John-Albert:
That section 50, subsection 1, be further amended by changing the figures "6 per cent" and "7 per cent" where they occur in lines eighteen and twenty-three thereof to read "4 per cent" and "6 per cent" respectively.
I might point out that I am using the figure "7 per cent" there because the minister indicated that was the correct one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is the same amendment, of course, which was ruled out of order when this bill was before the house; and I do not intend to repeat the arguments which I made then as to why it is out of order. I frankly find it difficult to see why people are so much exercised about the difference between four per cent and six per cent interest to people who do not pay their taxes in full. It was six per cent for many years until a couple of years ago.
It never should have been.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps. But after having reduced that rate to four per cent, we found that advantage was being taken of it by a good many people in this country who felt that this was a nice, cheap way of getting an unsecured loan from the government at four per cent per annum. Not only do they do that by filing their tax returns, showing a certain amount of tax payable and then not paying the full amount of tax, knowing the assessment department will not be able to assess the return for a year or two; but a great many people, who are not quite so scrupulous as the ones to whom I have just referred, will charge in a great many expenses which they know or have reason to believe will probably be disallowed when the department gets around to assessing the return. But of course that will be eighteen months or a couple of years from now, and in the meantime they will have had the use of the money at four per cent. This provision is put in to prevent abuses of that kind; and, so far as I am concerned, I shall insist that it stay in the law.

I can tell the minister why some people are exercised because of this sort of thing. It is because they have seen an injustice done to perfectly honest taxpayers who have made what they regarded as an honest assessment. Their revised assessment has not been received for two or three years after they turned it in; and they were then charged interest when, through no fault of their own, they are in arrears on the payment of their taxes. That is why people get exercised, because they see perfectly honest taxpayers subjected to an interest penalty because
Income Tax Act

the department itself is in arrears in making the revised assessment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let them make their tax returns out correctly.

As was pointed out by the minister in the argument he put forward, if there are people who assess themselves at one sum, and then send in a cheque for a smaller sum, thus taking advantage of the situation which he outlined, there can be no objection to charging them the full interest rate. But in the case of the great average mass of taxpayers-probably 1,999,000 out of 2,000,000 taxpayers-who make their assessments honestly and who pay in full, I suggest that it is unfair to penalize them because there may be some who take advantage of a loophole in the tax law. I am not so concerned about the wealthy man-
Oh, oh.

-who takes advantage of the law and who may be penalized or may be charged the full interest rate. Let the minister bring in an amendment to deal with him. But I am concerned about the man who tries to be honest, and who is simply set against government in all forms because he finds himself unjustly treated by the department against which he has no recourse. Hon. members across the way may say, "Oh, oh", if they like. Of course one cannot go fully into the motives which cause one to move amendments or to make suggestions, but I say that is what I have in mind in moving this amendment. I do not think it is a matter to be shrugged off; nor is it a matter, I suppose, about which one should get heated, especially when one finds in one's own experience, as I am sure all hon. members have found-because no hon. member is unique in this or any other respect-that honest taxpayers are penalized through no fault of their own. So I think we should try to draw up such amendments as will prevent these hardships being inflicted upon them.

There is one aspect of this situation I should like to draw to the attention of the minister. When six per cent was the rate previously it was the normal rate, which applied almost universally. Today the interest rate is much lower. One can borrow for three and three and a half per cent-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not on unsecured loans.
-and four per cent, with reasonable security.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not on unsecured loans.

I hope the taxpayer is not considered as other than good security. After all, the taxpayer is the security of Canada, and it is that aspect of the situation I am asking the minister to consider. Really the rates of six and seven per cent today are equivalent to ten and twelve per cent at the time these penalties were originally imposed. They become penalties, in fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Anyone can avoid the payment of these rates by preparing a proper income tax return and paying the amount of the tax due. I am just as solicitous as anyone else for the average taxpayer; but the taxpayer I am particularly solicitous about is the one who honestly makes up his return, accurately computes his tax, and pays it when due; and that taxpayer does not pay any interest.

Then why does not the minister provide a category for these nefarious people, who apparently must be numerous, or he would not be passing legislation to fit, them? Why does he not prepare a class which will include them? Why should the ninety-nine innocent people suffer because of the one who is not as careful as he might be in paying his tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is a very good lawyer, but if he could draw up a clause
I am v'illing to help.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -which would accurately describe a taxpayer who claims an expense which is subsequently disallowed, and prove that this claim was made intentionally, he is better than I think he is.

But that is the basis of the hon. gentleman's argument, that there are people who are doing this intentionally, in order that they may benefit improperly and dishonestly through it. I say, let us deal with them; but why treat the ordinary individual who makes up his return, sends in what he believes he owes and then wakes up perhaps twenty months later-it cannot be longer than that, because the interest does not run beyond that period-to find that he owes the government a substantial sum? I suggest to the minister that good business warrants some segregation, some selection between those who pay readily and willingly all they believe they owe, and those who fall into the category the minister has described.

As far I know, Mr. Chairman. you did not rule on the point of order. Before you do so I should like to say I do not

Income Tax Act
think the minister's point is well taken. If this is a deterrent; if fewer people will pay the interest, you are likely to collect more taxes with the six per cent and four per cent than with the six per cent and eight per cent. So I do not think the minister has made a case at all. If this is to be a deterrent to people underpaying their taxes I think he is away out, so I believe you might very well rule the amendment in order.
I think the hon. member for Kamloops and the hon. member for Stanstead have made a fairly good case here. The principle the minister is adopting is that he is going to punish a man who has done something without premeditation, if that is the word, or without intent, in the same way that he is going to punish a man who did the same thing with intent. Surely that is a bad principle. While there is nothing I hate more than a chiseler I do not think you should punish the person who has made a mistake in the same way as you punish the person who has defrauded with intent. That is exactly what is being done in this case.
While I am speaking on this subject, though it may not have anything to do with the particular section, I believe the income tax branch is extremely negligent in returning moneys that have been overpaid. I do not want to raise a personal question, but I made an overpayment on my 1942 tax, and I did not get it back until 1948, after considerable correspondence. I received no interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You will from now on.

As far as the department was concerned, very likely I would never have got it back. I do not know how they keep their records, but I do say that in this instance you are penalizing the person who inadvertently underpays his income tax in the same way as you are penalizing a person who has done so writh intent.

I have to agree with my leader in this instance. When this clause was discussed in the house before the bill went to committee I pointed out to the minister that there were instances of hardship in the application of interest, where taxes were wrongly computed. The person who suffers most under this section is, in my opinion, the industrial worker, ninety per cent of whose tax is supposed to be collected at the source. He keeps no record himself; but, through broken time and time lost through sickness, the records of the company are at fault in many cases. At the end of April, when he comes to file his return, he is not really in a position to figure his tax. So he makes a guess at it, an honest guess. That
return may lie in the income tax office for fifteen months, and at the end of that time he may get a bill for $75, $100 or $200 which he had no idea he owed; not a large amount, mind you, for the class of people my hon. friends to the right are thinking about-
That is very unfair.

-but a lot of money for the fellow who is making only $1,200 or $1,500 a year and paying his tax. It is absolutely unfair to collect interest in a case of that kind, and I believe the collection of this interest might very well be dropped. Very reluctantly I agree with hon. gentlemen to the right on that. I believe section 126, which we just passed-and I hope the minister has not weakened it by accepting the amendment-is a kitchen-sink clause which might very well take care of the category some of my hon. friends are trying to protect.
Why assume that? I think you had better take that back.
Be a sport and take it back.
I never take anything back, and I do not say anything I do not mean.

My hon. friend is a good lawyer. Any time he is retained either to defend or to prosecute, the first thing he gropes for is a motive. I am suggesting, Mr. Chairman, that in prosecuting this particular section the motive is profit. I think my assumption is fairly reasonable.
Your assumption is only a C.C.F. assumption, and it is not worth anything.
That is scarcely the view taken by people who elected members to the House of Commons and the legislature. Some people do not agree with you.
If you use that kind of method to get them in, I do not doubt you can get them in under false pretenses.

It is not false pretenses. People are smartening up; they are getting wise to you.
I have pointed out that the case of a serviceman who had enlisted in 1942 with an income w'hich placed him in the income tax brackets. He went overseas ' and returned in 1945. He was billed interest for the years he was actually overseas in the services. The income tax officials had no alternative, front

The rate of interest should be dropped. I know, as the minister has said, that all the details cannot be written into legislation. I hope that when the regulations are being prepared some provision will be made whereby the departmental officials will have the necessary latitude to make adjustments where there are extenuating circumstances such as I have outlined.

Mr. Speaker, may I bring to the attention of the house a matter which I consider of major national importance? I hold in my hand an invoice in respect of a keg of four-inch nails bought in the city of Toronto at the price of $16.75.
Oh, oh.

This may be a matter of laughter to some members, but I think the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply will thank me for bringing it to his attention and he will probably act on the information which I intend1 to submit to the house. Actually a keg of four-inch nails costs $5.85 if it could be bought, but this particular keg cost $16.75, which represents an increase of about 300 per cent. Not only have I the invoice, but I have here the keg of nails.
The minister has told us on previous occasions that sometimes these nails come across the border from the United States and that he has no control over the price that may be
Nails

obtained for American nails. That is so, but this keg of nails, which is in the lobby and can be produced, bears the stamp of the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation, Sydney, Nova Scotia, and Montreal. Evidently, therefore, this keg of nails was produced in Canada and was on the market to be sold in the ordinary course of events.
On May 10 last at page 3774 of Hansard I asked a question of the minister of reconstruction regarding this matter. On that occasion I said:
Builders in Toronto are in a desperate position in regard to nails. Representations have been made to the minister's department to see what can be done to cut through whatever obstacles are holding up production. Apparently at the present time the wire is not available, and I understand that the minister has control of the disposition of wire materials to various firms.
I will not read the rest of it. The minister at the time replied, quite properly:
I have asked our people to give all the preference they dare to give to nails, and we are going to take a bite out of wire products. There will be complaints about that, but you cannot distribute more than there is in toto. We are in process of diverting wire from other uses into nails. We are not going to make any barbed wrire for a few months. I hope hon. members who have been worrying about nails will not start worrying about other products, because that is the only way to get more nails.
In fairness to the minister, it must be said that he did follow the matter up, and on June 1 the steel controller issued a directive or order of his department under that date. Without going into any details, I may say he did direct the ^teel producers to increase production on nails, and as a matter of fact a great many more nails have been produced. The minister will agree with me that those nails were for house builders. That was why he urged the increased production of nails. The fact is, however, that the nails are not going to home builders, and it is my purpose to try to satisfy the house and the minister that something must be done about the matter.
I was in touch with the steel controller, and he told me frankly thalt the bottleneck in respect of getting nails to home builders was that down to the level of the wholesaler distribution was fair and equitable, but when it got away from the wholesaler there was trouble and he was trying to do what he could to find ways and means of setting a pattern for getting nails into the hands of the builders themselves.
What brought this whole thing about was an advertisement which appeared in a paper in Portage la Prairie about two or three weeks ago. There was an advertisement of 10,000

kegs of steel nails which were available, all sizes. The advertisement read:
Nails-steel-10,000 kegs available of all sizes. Write for price list. Sherman's box 1005, postal station "C", Toronto, Can.
After having received that particular clipping, I had an investigation made by some members of the National House Builders' Association of Toronto. The result was that they purchased this keg of nails for $16.75. But not only did we find that advertisement in the Toronto paper; we found these others. Plere is one:
Nails! Nails! Nails!
Nails, common, steel, 2} inch, 3 inch, 4 inch, $14.50 per keg. 3534 Duiulas St. W., MU. 4815, open daily 8 to 8.
That was followed by another advertisement:
Nails
$16.75 per keg, common steel lj inch, 2 inch, 21 inch, 3 inch, 4 inch and 6 inch. Finishing nails slightly higher. LA. 2823, 1275 Queen St. W.
That, Mr. Speaker, is right in my own district of Parkdale. Nails are being sold at $16.75 a keg. That was followed by another advertisement:
Nails, steel, common, finishing, 624 Bloor St. W. LL. 3200.
That is also in the city of Toronto. As a matter of fact, this leakage with respect to the distribution of nails to home builders is not just an isolated case. Here was another advertisement which mentions 10,000 kegs of nails.
A friend of mine who was making the investigation said he saw in the garage where he bought his nails, 100 or 200 kegs of nails which were available for sale. There is certainly a hole in the administration with respect to the distribution of these nails. It is quite apparent that among our citizens there is a good deal of chiseling going on. There are a great many small-town chiselers who are running up the cost of building in this country.
Big town.

All right; big town, if you like. There are a great many small chiseling people who are doing these things. I am saying to the minister that something ought to be done and ought to be done right away. I am quite prepared to hand these advertisements to the minister. He ought to have an investigation made tomorrow because, just as soon as this gets in the press, these people will be closing up shop. But the nails are there in Toronto, and if these people are guilty of chiseling on the people who want to build homes, then we should act at once. As

Nails
I understand it, in the wartime prices and trade board order there is a section which says that if you sell above what is fair and reasonable, you are committing a crime. Certainly 300 per cent is not fair and reasonable. AVe all know that. I am bringing this to the attention of the minister. I am not criticizing him and I am not criticizing his department.
I know the steel controller has been trying to find some machinery by means of which to have these nails distributed properly. But some place along the line the system has broken down. Some place along the line there are those who are taking advantage of the Canadian people, and I ask the minister to give the matter immediate attention.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I can say to my hon. friend, Mr. Speaker, and I think he agrees, that no other feature of steel control has received the attention that the distribution of nails has received. I am certain that Canadian manufacturers are selling at fair and reasonable prices. I believe they are selling to reliable distributors, and I think to that extent we have found no flaw in the system. From the distributors down, some nails perhaps get into the wrong hands, although I think the distributors are most conscientious in attempting to distribute the nails to reliable or bona fide users.
I have said before that nails are brought in from the United States and sold here. In the United States nails cost nearly twice as much as they do in Canada, which is a tribute to the fact that we have kept our steel production in order from a price viewpoint. These nails are brought in and distributed at a profit. I said that I saw no particular harm in that. If anyone is so desperate or so pressed for nails that, rather than wait for nails at the Canadian price of about $5.80 a keg, he must pay $16.50; and if they are not Canadians nails; if they are nails in addition to the Canadian product-
If the house would like me to bring in the keg, I will do so; and it does not say they are United States nails.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
No. The hon. member
undoubtedly has a keg of nails that was manufactured in Canada, handed down through our distribution system, diverted into the wrong hands and is being resold at an exorbitant profit. If we could learn the history of that transaction we would, of course, prosecute. But I think the remarkable thing is that, of all the nails distributed, it is one keg that we are talking about.
If the minister will pardon me for interrupting, this firm that sold these nails advertised that they had 10,000 kegs of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
AVe will make an investigation; and if there are 10,000 kegs of Canadian nails, I can assure my hon. friend a prosecution will foe launched tomorrow.
The hon. member made one other statement that I think I should correct. He said the additional nails we are making out of wire that was formerly put into fencing wire and barbed wire are not going inlto housing. I can assure him definitely that those nails are going into housing, because they are being distributed to house builders through government agencies. Those nails definitely do go into housing. The former pattern has not been changed for the former production, but the government has commandeered excess production and is taking its own methods to make sure that it all goes inlto house building.

While the hon. member is considering his comment, with his permission this may be a -good opportunity for me to answer some questions that were asked just before we rose last evening, shortly after eleven o'clock.

I am told that no grant has been made in any of these cases; but I understand that the members of the Indian band residing on the reserve on which Pauline Johnson was born have been contemplating from time to time the erection of some kind of memorial. The department is naturally interested in this proposal and welcomes the initiative being taken by the band.

The hon. member for Kamloops inquired as to the reason for the delay in tabling the annual report of the Department of Mines and Resources for the year ended March 31, 1947. This matter has been checked, and I find that final proof of the report was sent to the king's printer several weeks ago. Its production has been delayed by the heavy load of sessional publications with which the king's printer has had to contend. It is the hope of the department that the next annual report will be prepared at such an early date that there will be no doubt as to its being available to members of parliament while the house is still in session. I should add that the report of this department, containing as it does a summary of a great deal of scientific material, is necessarily a slow and difficult document to produce.
The hon. member for Danforth and the hon. member for Calgary West questioned me about the well which had run out of control in the Leduc sector of the Edmonton field'. It was indicated by one hon. member that this well had been brought under control. Unfortunately, on checking this matter, I found that we had received airmail advice yesterday to the effect that the well is still pouring out from ten to fifteen thousand barrels a day. Steps have been taken to pump some six thousand barrels of this oil back into the ground in a safe area, but as yet the situation is by no means satisfactory. Production in the field, apart from this one well, is almost at a standstill.
The hon. member for York South asked for figures relating to the number of departmental employees this year as compared with a year ago in the mines, forests and scientific services branch, or in the legal survey division; I was not altogether clear as to which was desired. speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: I quite understand the reasons that have prompted the hon. member to make these comments; but the projects to which he refers are projects which are being considered by my colleague the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. Why is that put in?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext:
That is a heading which is used in the department. There have been purchases of land in the past, and there will be in the future. But at the present time in this item there is no amount for the purchase of land and, may I say, very little for the construction of buildings. To a great extent these items are for the construction of highways in the parks which fell into disrepair during the war years when practically no money was spent on park development.
The necessity for proceeding with this work has been well known to the government. It has been urged on us from all sides in Canada
as an encouragement to United States tourists to come to our parks and spend their dollars on vacations here. I am sure, when the hon. member sees the items in Hansard, he will approve them.

My point in rising was to get the details, so that the committee itself could judge as to the necessity for proceeding with the work at the present time. I am not criticizing having this work done to attract tourists.

For some years past I have been calling the attention of the government to this item. The report the minister gave was a very good one, as far as it went. However I would call his attention to the situation which prevails in the chief tax producing provinces of the dominion,
I am not objecting to these historic parks and sites in other provinces; far from it. I believe in a policy of national parks and historic sites. But I find that Ontario has been overlooked for many years. For example, we have no large national park in the whole province. We have small islands near lake Ontario in the St. Lawrence river, one up at Pelee island, and parks of that kind.
But we must consider what a great investment these national parks can be. Let us have in mind the Rideau lakes district. The Rideau canal was constructed by the British government after the war of 1812 as a backdoor to lake Ontario, and was paid for by the British taxpayers. A magnificent chain of rivers, lakes and streams connects with the canal system. Many people see it while they drive along in their automobiles. That canal system could be linked up with the great chain of lakes and with the inland waterways. In the Trent district we have the Murray canal, and a canal system reaching right up the Severn into the Muskoka district. Then, it is possible to link up the lake Simcoe district, the Muskoka district, the Parry Sound district and that around Georgian bay with the district at the head of lake Ontario. Parks in those areas should be connected. They would be crown property, held eitheT in the right of the province or in the right of the Minister of Public Works for the dominion.
These parks should be linked up into a great chain of public parks so as to attract tourist revenue, not only in the summer months, but also in the winter when winter sports in those park areas wouildi be possible.
I believe Ontario has been overlooked. I have in mind old Fort Henry, in the Kingston area. It is, no doubt, an historic site. At the time the minister visited the coliseum during
Supply-Mines and Resources

the time of the magnificent international trade fair within recent weeks, he probably knows that opposite the place where the fair was held is a fort which wras taken by the Americans in the war of 1812-14. There is no reason why some money should not be spent on that fort, and something done along the lines of what has been done at Fort Henry.
I suggest that during the parliamentary recess the minister might consider what is said to him by a deputation which has been appointed by the city council in Toronto to interview him. One must remember that the city has spent about $26,000,000 in grounds, buildings and permanent exhibits in connection with the Canadian National exhibition.
As one of the main contributors in the matter of taxation, Ontario should receive further consideration, because that province has been overlooked. One might mention the historic site and battlefields of the war of 1812-14 which are to be found in the Niagara district. The Ontario government has taken care of some of them. But there are many other points connected with the first and second great wars which should have recognition. I have in mind places where our troops were trained. The government should have a policy of seeking out, in every military district of the country, the sites where the soldiers were trained before they went overseas.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: 208. Wildlife resources conservation and developments, including administration of the Migratory Birds Convention Act, $181,360.

I am afraid that this is one branch of the minister's department which needs a bit of checking over. This is the branch which looks after predatory animals. Recently I was in Essex county and paid a visit to Point Pelee. There I was interviewed by quite a number of residents, who called to my attention the destruction in the park, which could be much more beautiful than it is if it were properly taken care of. In fact it is the only national park in western Ontario. I commend the park to the minister's attention. It should be beautified; but, above all, the first thing that should be done is to kill the predatory animals in the park. All the farmers around about are complaining about the department encouraging the maintenance of the predatory animals such as wolves, red foxes and coyotes, which are destroying the pheasants and other so-called wild but harmless animals. The Leamington Post and News of June 17 had this to say:
People who do not believe in the control of predatory beasts are invited to visit Point Pelee national park adjacent to Leamington, Ontario. Here exists at the present time, one of the best possible demonstrations of what happens when animals that prey upon other animal life are not killed.
In every one of the nine provinces of Canada, it is the policy of the provincial government to foster an increase in the number of deer within its borders. They are wanted for food for humanity. Most of the provinces, therefore encourage the slaughter of wolves and coyotes by paying a bounty of several dollars for each one killed, while several counties in Ontario pay a bounty also on red foxes.
In the federal parks within these provinces, the dominion government, under the management of the federal fish and game department, protects all predators, and any man would be prosecuted for shooting a coyote, wolf, or red fox inside such a federal park.
A few years ago pheasants were so plentiful around this Leamington national park that citizens took motion pictures of them from their cars as they motored through the park. Then

coyotes and red foxes came in and, under the policy of the dominion government, were given the protection referred to. Farmers living within the boundaries of the park were even notified to keep their dogs chained up-which certainly did not make sense to them while coyotes were being permitted to run at large without molestation.
I have had quite a number of letters from that beautiful county, no more beautiful county in Canada, and I am going to ask the minister to take this under his control. I say to him that if anyone in his department is protecting wolves and coyotes in this park, I would ask him to tell him to take a walk somewhere else. He should not be in the department helping to maintain the national parks.

I wish to say a few words in connection with one species of wildlife, namely ducks and geese, because one might put these two birds together. There is an article in Rod <fc Gun, which is taken from Field and Stream and which is headed: "Can our duck shooting be saved?" This magazine says, "Ares, but the remedy must be drastic." Duck shooting is a great sport, but the duck population of this country is going down and down. We have had limits on the number of ducks that a man is allowed to take in a day, and the number he can have in his possession and so on. We have associations such as "Ducks Unlimited". I wish there were; I wish we had ten Ducks Unlimited, so that the duck population might be increased. There are a lot of factors that enter into the matter. There are 400,000 more hunters than there used to be, and it is easier to get to the duck-shooting grounds. There are two or three solutions of the problem; but, as I say, drastic measures must be taken, or there will not be any ducks. The article goes on to say:
Protection came too late for only one, the Eskimo curlew. It took twenty to twenty-five years for our gulls, terns, shore birds, herons, egrets, ibises and cormorants to become common once more. During the same period the abolition of spring shooting of ducks produced tangible results in five years.
The article goes on to say:
So great is the vigour and fertility of our waterfowl that I honestly believe a five-year closed season would quadruple their numbers.
There is no doubt about it, if we had a closed season. I do not know that it is possible to have it. There is no doubt that the future of our waterfowl shooting depends upon the ability to secure the necessary knowledge and to finance the techniques which have been worked out, and of hunters to exercise enough selfrestraint; but I do not think sufficiently drastic action has been taken.

Supply-Mines and Resources
I wonder whether there is sufficient co-operation by the people of the United States. It is no use our breeding ducks here in our north country and then having them slaughtered in the south. I know that there is co-operation between the two countries. I do not know that there is co-operation between the various states. For instance, they will have a closed season in one flight lane and the shooters all go over to the other lane. That is not having a closed season. For the benefit of this country I wish, if it might be possible, that we could arrange with the United States to have a closed season for, say two years, on the shooting of ducks in both the United States and Canada. That would make a tremendous difference.
Ducks increase in geometrical proportion. They come back very quickly, but unless we take drastic action there will be no duckshooting for anyone. These birds can be preserved. The Jack Miner foundation is doing its best in its small way. It, gets $5,000 a year, but grain has gone up and it would be a good idea to give it a little more money. This is one of the most important things in our country, because we must preserve our wild life, and particularly our wild bird life. It is a great asset to, the country; but, as I say, unless w'e do something drastic, we shall find ourselves without any ducks in a short time.
I commend to the minister this article in the magazine Rod & Gun. It appears in the last number, the June issue. The minister comes from a duck-shooting country and perhaps he has been out many times. I, too, used to be fond of shooting. It is a fine sport and I want to see it saved for the young people of Canada; but, unless we take the necessary steps, there will be no ducks left in the country.

In the matter of
Indian affairs, probably one's first words should be words of commendation to the former minister on the progress made on this important question of Canadian Indians, and I hope that the present minister will get a picture of the responsibility and the opportunity which exists in regard to emancipating these unfortunate people who are within our gates and who find themselves the wards of this government.
May I express appreciation of what has been done within the last three years and since a committee was set up to deal with the revision of the Indian Act? That committee has done valuable work, and its findings have revealed shocking conditions among the
130,000	human beings who live within the
Supply-Mines and Resources

borders of the country. My complaint is that, in spite of what has been done, it is too little, too late and much too slow.
The condition among the Indians calls for immediate redress. We can no longer stall or wait. The matter demands action from this government. It requires the revision of the act and drastic action within the department, on the part of those responsible for the administration of Indian affairs.
The majority of these people at the present time live under conditions of poverty, want, disease and ignorance. There are a few bright spots where conditions are better, such as Caughnawaga, the Six Nations reserve, some in Alberta and a few on the western coast of British Columbia where the Indians are engaged in fishing. Some of them are doing very well. We must not forget that these people are human beings, and under the present set-up they have no control over their own destiny, no say in their own government, no say about their own affairs. They have limited approach toward justice; they are not able to pay for legal advice. The conditions among many of these people, particularly in the backward areas, are such that the reserves on which they are compelled to live are not sufficiently well supplied with natural resources to provide them with a decent standard of living. In many cases they lack the necessary assistance to make a start in providing for themselves.
Years of protest and complaint have finally brought about the setting up of a committee of this house, which has revealed a shocking state; and it is time, now that we know enough about the matter, to do something about rectifying some of the basic wrongs. We find from the records that 18,000 Indian children are receiving some kind of education, either in residential or in day schools, but the shocking condition is revealed that 12,000 Indian children are receiving no training whatever. After sixty years of administration in this country, to have these facts facing us is a revelation as to how serious the situation is and how completely the Indians have failed to accept responsibility in this regard.
The whole hope of the future of the Indians must he in our ability to train them adequately. I am pleased that something is being done, that there are some signs of improvement, and that the government is already spending some larger sum in education. There are signs of progress. As I said before, I am pleased at the amount of money which is being spent by the Department of Health and Welfare to make a survey of the situation with regard to health among our Indians, with a

view to doing something about remedying the condition of these people. I think the evidence given before the committee would show that these Indians have the capacity to become fine citizens-they are fine people; they have excellent qualities-if they are only given an opportunity. I think the evidence will reveal that the Canadian Indian is a sick man. Until we remedy the economic position, health conditions and conditions of training among them, we cannot hope to solve this problem.
The fact of the matter is that the actual training of the Indians does not suit them for the bind of life they must live. Many of them go to residential schools, learn how to live under modern conditions, return to their reserves after they have reached the age of sixteen and find that they do not like to go back to their terrible housing and living conditions on the reserve. However, they find themselves unable to take their position in the modern white man's way of life, and they seem to become lost between two worlds. They sink down into a hopeless condition, and few of them really make a success or show any of the signs of progress which we would hope for.
There is another thing which reveals something which I think is basically wrong with our treatment of these people. For instance, there has recently been considerable discussion about the matter of granting the franchise to Canadian Indians. One of the big troubles with regard to this matter has been that the Indians themselves are not taken into the confidence of those who are administering their affairs. They only hear that a report has been tabled in this house stating that it is the intention of a committee or a group of people to recommend to the house that the franchise be granted. The Indian wants to know what that entails. Does it mean that they are to become citizens of Canada? Does it mean that they are to lose any of the rights or privileges which they have enjoyed under the treaties? If it means that they are to lose their treaty rights, the Indians themselves do not want to have much to do with it. A great many of them are suspicious of those who administer their affairs, because they have not been taken properly into the confidence of those people. The Indians should have been brought into consultation with those who administer their affairs, told of these suggestions and been allowed to know exactly what the Canadian people intended to do.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

Yes.

My hon. friend is a member of this committee. He has brought this subject up.
What is the hon. member's question?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.
I am coming to my question.
It is a speech.

The hon. member has brought this question up. Will he now tell us the means and methods whereby he would have the Indians represented on the Indian affairs committee? He has not done so in the last two years.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Oh, let us get on.

As I believe the hon. member, who is chairman of that committee, knows very well, the Indians appeared before this committee and representations were brought before the committee. There are Indian organizations across this country in each of the provinces, in each of the divisions ){ Canada; and they hold annual conventions. There is an organization of Indians across the whole of Canada which could quite quickly, with a little bit of assistance, choose those who could speak for them. It would be quite possible to have representatives from the Indian groups across Canada sit in with this committee, with watching briefs, to talk over the matter and give the Indian viewpoint. I think I mooted that procedure at the early meetings of the committee, but the committee voted my recommendation down.
It is most important that, if we are to suggest any such thing, the Indians should be given every assurance that the granting of any franchise would in no way interfere with any of t'heir rights. It is quite evident also that the Indians are suspicious of this, and some of them have already stated that they do not want to have anything to do with it. As a matter of fact, they do not know what it entails and are naturally suspicious; and such a thing would vitally affect them.
The matter of treaties and of the rights and privileges under treaties requires immediate remedy. The recommendations of the committee that were recently tabled in this house should be adopted by this house and implemented by the department, particularly with regard 'to the setting up of a claims commission. The matter of hundreds of treaties, under which the various Indians in various groups across Canada are now living, requires adjustment. In my own province of Saskatchewan it has been revealed that
the original reserves set aside for the Indians occupy considerable territory in different parts of that province. Since those reserves were set aside, it is a matter of fact that some 400,000 acres have been taken away from them and have been either sold to white people ox used in other ways. Those reserves are, in reality, the property of the Indians. They were set aside in order that the Indians might make a livelihood upon them. If we would look over the terms of the original treaties, we would find that it was certainly the intent of those treaties that the Indian should be properly cared for, that he should be properly trained, and that the great white mother or queen, who was ruling this country at that time, would see that the Indian was properly recompensed and properly cared for as a result of this surrender of these vast territories.
The Indian resents the position of inferiority in which he is placed. The Indian is a noble being. It has been revealed that under proper conditions he has remarkable capacity, a fine intellect and certainly excellent qualities of character. I do not think he has been improved by his contact with the white man in every instance. I suggest that a change is needed in the attitude of the white Canadian people toward these our red brothers. I believe that ultimately we shall have to take these people into our confidence, treat them as equals and give them an opportunity to share in the making of their own destiny.

As a member from a Vancouver constituency where the condition of the Indians in our area is particularly pressing, I should like to add my voice in support of the remarks made by my colleague. I should like to draw to the minister's attention the remarks made earlier in this debate or on this report by the hon. member for Nanaimo.
In the Vancouver newspapers last winter appeared a great number of letters, which were written by citizens, about the conditions of the Indians in British Columbia and about the conditions in the Indian schools. It appears that in these schools the boys and girls are completely segregated and are not permitted to speak to one another at all in the classrooms during the school day. They eat separately and are treated in an entirely different way from children of the same age of our own race. This type of old-fashioned regimentation in schools is producing in the Indian mind a psychology at variance with the general outlook of the average white child, and they are growing up with peculiarities which set them apart from the rest of

Supply-Mines and Resources
the population to a greater extent than would be caused by any matter of pigmentation or racial background.
At the University of British Columbia, where I was recently a student, Indian students are as brilliant and capable as any others. During the last term a representative of the native brethren came to address the student body. He spoke clearly, in an educated manner, and presented the case for the Indians. From the floor of that meeting the question was raised as to whether the Indians desired the franchise; that is the very point which was brought up by the hon. member who spoke previously this evening. The reply of the Indian who was addressing the meeting was that they wanted the franchise, but if it were to cost them privileges and treaty rights, then something would have to be added to the franchise to make it worthwhile from their point of view.
I should like to ask the minister if he is aware of the situation with respect to Indian girls from the Capilano reserve in North Vancouver, who come to the city and go along that street we call the skid road, otherwise known as Cordova street. There they are taken into hotel rooms by various people and debauched; and many are found in these rooms with liquor in their possession. According to newspaper reports, hardly a day goes by that some man is not prosecuted for this type of crime. No doubt the minister has this information; and I hope and trust that everything possible will be done to remedy that condition, by one method or another. Every effort is made locally to keep down crimes of this kind; and, since these people are wards of the government and a federal responsibility, every co-operation should be given by this department.
I should like to ask whether there has been any suggestion that this country should follow the example set by New Zealand, where Liberal and Conservative governments have made possible direct representation of the aborigines in the parliament of the country, so that their conditions may be made known, their requests met and their needs fulfilled. It was suggested by one hon. member that some method might be found whereby Indian organizations could send representatives to meet with a parliamentary committee, and I would strongly urge that such a policy be adopted in future, if at all possible.
Some time ago I was ruled out of order when I sought to take up with the minister the matter of the payments now being made by the department to Indians over the age of seventy. I refer particularly to a recent increase of S8 a month, in addition to the $5 which originally was presented to these

Indians in the form of necessities by the Indian agent. I would appeal to the minister and the department to do whatever can be done to bring this amount more in line with the needs of the people receiving it. I feel that it is a deep disgrace to our country that this situation has been permitted to continue for so long. I do not suggest that it is done deliberately. I cannot believe that; but I believe we as a nation have been guilty of neglect. Whether neglect is as great a crime as deliberate intention, in this particular case the crime is almost as great; and in the interests of the country at large, the whole attitude of the department and of the federal government should be changed and a more humanitarian ideal pursued in the treatment of our native peoples.
I want to make one last reference to the schools in which the majority of the Indian boys and girls in my province are educated at the present time. It has been suggested that the teachers employed in schools which are under private charitable auspices are not up to the standard, and in fact are definitely below the standard, of the teachers in the ordinary public schools, and that this is partly due to the fact that the organizations employing them pay smaller salaries, on the average, than they could obtain in the ordinary schools. If this is the case, as we have reason to believe it is; if it is the policy to employ the cheapest teachers, who perhaps are not able to fill ordinary posts in the public schools, and give them to the Indians, there is every reason to suppose that the Indian children will not develop to the point where they can be regarded as normal Canadian citizens.	Such a policy is
extremely detrimental to the development of the Indian from his present position to one of responsibility as a fellow citizen.

Our Indian policy in Canada is far short of what it should be. While the committee on the Indian Act has been at work for three years, I seriously fear that the net result of all our efforts will be exceedingly disappointing, not only to the Indians but to Canadians at large. I do not wish to be unduly critical; I intend to be constructive. The minister should set out on a definite, progressive policy with regard to our Indians, and should not be afraid to spend money. It seems to me that up to the present time our whole policy with regard to Indians has been to see how niggardly we could treat them, how small a sum of money we could spend on them. That is not the way to make a great people.
I am going to suggest several things, though I do not wish to delay the committee unduly.

Supply-Mines and Resources
In the first place, I believe a revolving fund of around 150,000,000 should be established from which, under the direction and with the advice of Indian councils and government agencies, Indians would be able to borrow to establish themselves in farming or whatever activity they might desire to follow. This is a serious disability on the reservation in my constituency. Young people coming along have no means at all of obtaining cattle, for example, with which to start cattle raising, or to do anything else they want to do.
Another revolving fund ought to be established to enable less fortunate Indians to build moderately priced homes. And much care should be given, may I advise the minister, to the provision of an adequate water supply for our Indians. On the reservation I have the honour to represent, some Indians have, to haul water in barrels on a wagon for fifteen miles every other day in order to have a water supply at all. How in the world can they compete successfully if they have handicaps of that kind? That sort of thing must be overcome. I have been striving for some time to bring about some arrangement under which Indians might drill wells, but the department always seems to want the Indians to get the money from their own band funds. In many cases their band funds are almost negligible. I draw the minister's attention to this matter of a water supply definitely, because Indians suffer from unsuitable water just as much as white people would.
There should be a fund for providing scholarships for young Indians to enable them to attend colleges, universities and technical schools. Those scholarships should be real scholarships which would enable the young Indian people to go to school and enable them to hold their heads up among their fellows, and to participate in every way, just as our white young folks do.
We should examine into the possibility of establishing one or more Indian institutes or universities in which Indian history, Indian legends, Indian religions, Indian culture and Indian skills, arts, crafts and languages could be accumulated, learned and rendered available to young people, so that they could go there for a year or two and learn how their people lived in the past.
This matter has been neglected far too long. Many of the splendid Indian skills of fifty years ago have been almost entirely lost; I have in mind the tanning of skins, making of moccasins and the other crafts with which they were familiar. We should consider that the Indians have a great contribution to make to this country. They are a great race with a great past, and a great future. They are a
people with splendid characteristics. Indians are in no way inferior to white people, and in many respects they are superior to us. We should recognize that fact immediately, and govern their treatment with that in mind.
There should be a fund to help the Indians organize. We have just recently had a convention meeting of Indians here in Ottawa. Practically every Indian who bad anything to do with coming to the convention is financially hurt. They were not able to get the money with which to come here. There was no fund available. There should be a fund provided by the dominion government to help the Indians to organize provincially and on a dominion-wide basis. We must recognize that the Indians must learn to govern themselves in an Indian fashion.
Then, the matter of taxation of Indians is a disgrace to this country. Generally speaking, Indians have a very small chance to make good from an economic standpoint. I make that statement, judging by the Indians in my own province. When a particular Indian happens to get ahead a (bit he cannot return to the reserve with his money without the government coming in and taxing that money. I say that is an absolute disgrace to the country. It is disgraceful that Indians should be taxed on money they earn off the reserves. Surely, if we ourselves neglect the welfare of the Indian reserves to such a great extent we should let the Indians who go off the reserves and earn some money take it back and spend it in those reserves.
We should insist on a greater degree of Indian self-government. Every Indian effort to establish self-government throughout the country which would bring them in co-operation with the dominion government ought to be encouraged. I could tell stories of the last year which would reflect no great credit on the dominion government in respect of the way in which they have treated the Indian efforts to attempt self-government. Perhaps Indians have acted in a way which was just a little bit different from the way in which we think they should have acted. But when the Indians try to help themselves we should help them, not interfere with them.
The Indian claims commission suggested by the hon. member for Yorkton is a good suggestion. In the days of long ago the Indians had many privileges. They had the privilege of hunting, of fishing, of berrying, of logging and of grazing off the reserves, and to do those things freely on the reserves. When the treaties were entered into they were signed with the idea that the Indians would continue to have those privileges indefinitely.
Supply-Mines and Resources

Away back around 1875 no one ever dreamed that the area, for instance, south of the city of Calgary would be settled. It was assumed that the Indians would be able to take timber and to take the things they wished off the country. Now look where they are. They are confined to little pieces of territory. They have lost all their hunting, fishing, berrying and logging privileges. Where they used to make money from these activities, they cannot do so any more. There is hardly any other way for them to make money.
We simply must face this matter squarely and give it some more definite attention. Treaties were signed with the Indians, and those treaties should be recognized and observed by the dominion government. If they are not, then we shall build up a situation which will be dangerous for the future. We simply cannot go on disregarding these people as we have done in the past, because the day will come when they will become a problem and we shall not be very happy about it when they do.
For instance, in the matter of old age pensions, no one should have considered leaving the Indians out of the old age pensions scheme. Just imagine!-the people who are the least able to make their way have to be deprived of old age pensions, while those pensions are provided for the white population. We should have gone about the matter in exactly the opposite way. The Indians should have been the first to receive old age pensions. It is harder for an Indian to make money than for a white person. They should be receiving the old age pension at sixty years of age instead of at seventy.

We should give the Indians old age pensions right away and, as I say, at the age of sixty instead of at seventy. It should be done at once. They need it, and they need it badly in order to be able to nourish themselves.
Blind pensions should be just as generous for the Indians as for the white population. Other benefits should be just as generous. Family allowances should be more generous for Indians than for whites. We are giving them the same. But the ordinary Indian has nowhere near the facilities for making a living for his children that the white person has. I lived right alongside a reserve for fifty-six years, and for fifty of those years I was aware of the
TMr. Blackmore.]
way in which the Indians lived on their reserve. I have known that since I was eight years of age. I know the conditions under which they lived; and they were not good. The Indians should have had far more benefits.
I earnestly urge that the minister be not restricted in any way in any cheese-paring economy practices such as have been afflicting the committee on Indian affairs all the way through its deliberations. Let the minister consider the Indian Act, and make the report of the committee his point of beginning. I make these observations, knowing he will be sympathetic. He will have my complete support in any forward policy he may wish to introduce with respect to our Indian population.

It reads:
At the June session of the Brant county council, the following resolution was duly passed and is submitted herewith for your sympathetic consideration.
"Since the organization of the county of Brant, nearly one hundred years ago, it has had to pay for the administration of justice on an Indian reserve within its county. The county receives no taxes from this reserve, and as the Indian population here is 5,500 and the county's 24,800, it can be understood the administration of justice costs for Indian offenders is considerable, although they are law-abiding generally, but like other nationals they have many law breakers.
The province of Ontario pays for Indian offences on the same basis as for other indictable crown cases, but the Dominion of Canada, which is the guardian and trustee for moneys for these people, does not contribute any money for the maintenance of our courts, although representations have been made to various dominion governments over a period of eighty years, and each government appealed to has informed the county council that the administration of justice in each province is the responsibility of the provincial government, which in turn will only pay its normal proportion for all justice costs, claiming the Indians are wards of the Dominion of Canada and further costs will not be assumed by the province.
At the 1948 spring assizes, an Indian was convicted and sentenced to hang for a murder which occurred on the reservation, the costs of this trial were approximately $3,000-it is possible the county can recover $1,000 from the province in the normal way, the Brant county taxpayers, with those of the city of Brantford, will have to pay the balance, for as stated earlier, no taxes are paid into the county from the Indian reservation.
This is the second murder trial and conviction for an Indian in the past fifteen years, apart from other serious crimes.
We are asking each county council in Ontario to support Brant county in its appeal for more generous treatment by the dominion government, by writing to the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, Prime Minister of Canada; to the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley, Minister of Justice; the Hon. J. A. Glen, Minister of Mines and Resources, and to its local member of parliament, requesting the government to pay an equitable sum to all counties in which there is an Indian reservation, towards payment of administration of justice costs on that reservation."
We are also sending copies of this resolution to the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, Prime Minister of Canada, the Right Hon. Minister of Justice, the Hon. Minister of Mines and Resources, and W. Ross Macdonald, Esquire, M.P., Deputy Speaker of the House of Commons.
Yours very truly,
R. E. W. Lawrason.

I. wish to express my regret that such a meagre amount is being provided for the improvement of Indian reserves. I have already referred to the fact that $5,500,000 is being spent upon improvements and maintenance of our national parks for the benefit of tourists and Canadians on holiday. A few weeks ago the Minister of National Defence announced that $20 million will be spent to provide houses for members of our active forces who are married. I have no objection to that being done, but I object to only $500,000 being spent for the maintenance of the reserves and the provision of houses for our Indians.
I have brought to the attention of the department the details of the conditions that exist in my own constituency. I know whereof I speak, because I live next to an Indian reserve, and there are a number of smaller Indian reserves scattered throughout my district. There is one just outside Duncan, right on the highway. Any tourist driving up the the island highway must pass through Duncan and see the miserable hovels in which these Indians are living.
Then, right in the heart of Nanaimo is Nanaimo reserve No. 1. I went there last fall at the invitation of the chaplain of the reserve. I drove up to the boundary line and was told that I would have to leave my car. I stepped off a paved road onto a dirt track full of pot-holes. I left houses where there were electric lights, sewers and water, and I went in among hovels where there were no lights, no water, no sewers. This is right in the heart of Nanaimo beside a combined terminal for buses, rail and steamships upon which the Canadian Pacific are spending $2 million in order to attract tourists. The first thing a tourist will see will be the appalling conditions under which the Nanaimo Indians are living.

I pleaded with the department to do something to improve the roads, and they generously granted $100, making it $300 instead of $200 for the maintenance of roads. This enabled the Indians to bring in a few cartloads of cinders to put in the worst mud-holes. This is all I have been able to get from the department and it is not good enough. The Indians have pleaded that their houses be improved and that something be done to make their condition more satisfactory.
Another matter I brought to the attention of the department was the fact that the children on Nanaimo reserve No. 2. some eight miles away, have not been able to obtain any education for the last five or six years, simply and solely because the department will not bring the few Indian children on that reserve into the school at Nanaimo.
I do not care how long it takes to get these estimates through. I want the assurance from the minister that something will be done about that reserve before these estimates are passed.

Surely this is a ridiculous way to deal with these important estimates? At this late hour we are being kept here to pass them.
